questions.title: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Server. If two products are tied for the highest price, what number does each function give the row right after them?
questions.modelAnswer: All three are ranking window functions used with OVER(ORDER BY ...), and all three number rows based on the order you specify, but they disagree on what happens with ties. ROW_NUMBER() always assigns a unique, sequential integer to every row, even when two rows are tied on the ORDER BY column -- one of the tied rows arbitrarily gets the lower number. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but then skips ahead by the size of the tie: if two rows tie for rank 1, the next distinct row gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() is really counting 'how many rows came before or tied with me, plus one.' DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but the next distinct value gets the very next integer with no gap -- it's counting distinct values, not rows. So for two products tied for the most expensive: ROW_NUMBER gives them 1 and 2 (arbitrarily), RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 3, and DENSE_RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 2.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a concrete example because the difference only shows up when there's a tie. Say I'm ranking products by ListPrice and two products are tied for the top price. ROW_NUMBER() doesn't know about ties at all -- it just hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so the two tied products arbitrarily get 1 and 2. RANK() respects the tie -- both get rank 1 -- but it still 'reserves' a slot for each of them, so the next product down is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() is the one that feels most natural for something like a pricing tier: both tied products get 1, and the next distinct price is simply 2, no gap. In practice I reach for ROW_NUMBER() constantly for deduplication -- partition by the natural key, order by something like an ID, and anything with RowNum greater than 1 is a duplicate I can delete. I reach for RANK() when ties should genuinely cost a position, like a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for 2nd really does mean nobody is 3rd. And I reach for DENSE_RANK() when I just want the next distinct tier number and don't want gaps confusing anyone reading the report.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- If two products tie for the top ListPrice:
-- RowNum:     1, 2, 3, 4...  (ties broken arbitrarily)
-- Rank_:      1, 1, 3, 4...  (skips to 3 after the tie)
-- DenseRank_: 1, 1, 2, 3...  (no gap after the tie)
commonMistakes: Saying ROW_NUMBER() can produce duplicate numbers for ties (it never can -- it's always unique)
Mixing up which function skips numbers after a tie (it's RANK, not DENSE_RANK)
Forgetting that ROW_NUMBER() requires ORDER BY inside OVER() -- without it, row order is undefined
Not realizing all three still need PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily
RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead by the tie size afterward
DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number with no gap for the next distinct value
Choice depends on whether the business question treats a tie as 'costing' a rank

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes ROW_NUMBER's uniqueness behavior
Correctly describes RANK's gap-after-tie behavior
Correctly describes DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
questions.prompt: Explain what a transaction is in SQL Server, what COMMIT does that running the statements without a transaction wouldn't, and what exactly ROLLBACK undoes.
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction groups one or more statements into a single all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION marks the start of that group. Until COMMIT runs, the changes are provisional -- visible in the current session but not yet permanently saved, and still subject to being undone. COMMIT TRANSACTION makes every change inside the group permanent, all at once. ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION, as if none of it had ever happened. The reason this matters: a multi-step change (like moving stock from one location to another with two separate UPDATE statements) can fail halfway through if run as two independent statements, leaving the data in an inconsistent state. Wrapping both statements in a transaction guarantees either both succeed or neither does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I usually explain this with the classic example: moving inventory from warehouse A to warehouse B is really two UPDATEs -- subtract from A, add to B. If I just run those as two separate statements and the second one fails, I've got stock that's vanished into nowhere. A transaction fixes that by treating both statements as one all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the clock; until I COMMIT, those changes are provisional -- I can see them in my own session, but they're not durably saved and SQL Server can still throw them away. COMMIT makes them permanent. ROLLBACK is the safety net -- if something goes wrong partway through, it undoes everything back to the BEGIN, cleanly, as if I'd never run anything at all. The discipline I bring to it professionally is keeping transactions as short as possible, because every lock held inside one is held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK runs.
commonMistakes: Thinking changes inside a transaction are already permanent before COMMIT runs
Forgetting that ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN TRANSACTION, not just the most recent statement
Leaving a transaction open for a long time, holding locks and blocking other users unnecessarily
Not pairing every BEGIN TRANSACTION with a guaranteed COMMIT or ROLLBACK, even on the error path
keyPoints: A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of statements
Changes are provisional until COMMIT makes them permanent
ROLLBACK undoes everything since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION
Transactions exist to prevent partial, inconsistent multi-step changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a transaction groups together
Correctly explains what COMMIT does and the provisional state before it
Correctly explains the scope of what ROLLBACK undoes
Gives a realistic scenario showing why this matters

questions.title: What CALCULATE actually does
questions.prompt: Explain what the DAX CALCULATE function does, in one sentence, and then explain what happens by default when CALCULATE's filter argument targets a column that already has an active filter from a slicer.
questions.modelAnswer: CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context -- that's the whole function in one sentence, but nearly everything advanced in DAX is built on top of it. Its syntax is CALCULATE(<expression>, <filter1>, <filter2>, ...), where the expression is almost always a measure or an aggregation, and the filters narrow or change the filter context it's evaluated in. When a filter argument targets a column that isn't already filtered, the new filter is simply added. When the column is already filtered -- say, by a slicer -- CALCULATE's filter overwrites the existing one by default, rather than combining with it. This overwrite behavior is intentional: it's what lets you force an expression to ignore what a user selected and substitute your own condition instead.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain CALCULATE as the function that changes the rules an expression is evaluated under -- everything else in DAX that feels 'advanced,' from time intelligence to percent-of-total, is really just CALCULATE with a particular kind of filter passed into it. The syntax is simple: an expression first, then any number of filter arguments. The behavior that trips people up is what happens when a filter argument targets a column that's already filtered elsewhere, like a slicer on the report page. By default, CALCULATE doesn't combine with that existing filter -- it overwrites it entirely for that one expression. So if I write Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue"), and the report page already has a slicer set to 'Red,' that measure still shows blue-only revenue, because my CALCULATE filter replaced the slicer's filter rather than intersecting with it. That's deliberate and powerful -- but it's also the single most common source of 'why is my measure ignoring the slicer' confusion, which is exactly why KEEPFILTERS exists for the cases where you want the opposite behavior.
questions.example:
Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue")
-- Even with a report-level slicer on Product[Color] set to "Red",
-- this measure still returns blue-only revenue, because CALCULATE's
-- filter overwrites the slicer's filter on that same column by default.
commonMistakes: Describing CALCULATE only as 'a SUM with a filter' instead of the general filter-context-modification mechanism it is
Assuming a CALCULATE filter always combines with existing filters instead of overwriting them by default
Forgetting the filter argument can be a Boolean expression, a table expression (FILTER), or a filter modifier function
Not recognizing that time-intelligence functions and percent-of-total patterns are just CALCULATE under the hood
keyPoints: CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context
The filter argument can be a simple condition, a table expression, or a filter modifier
By default, a CALCULATE filter overwrites an existing filter on the same column, not combines with it
This overwrite behavior is what makes CALCULATE powerful for overriding user selections

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a correct one-sentence definition of CALCULATE
Correctly explains the default overwrite behavior on an already-filtered column
Provides a correct, relevant example

questions.title: Context transition in a calculated column
questions.prompt: A calculated column on a Customer table classifies each customer as 'High' or 'Low' value by calling CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey])) and comparing it to 2500. Explain how this can possibly work, given that a calculated column only ever sees row context.
questions.modelAnswer: This works because of context transition: whenever CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside row context, DAX converts that row context into an equivalent filter context, restricted to just that row's values. For one specific customer row, the row context (this one CustomerKey) becomes a filter context, as if the whole model had been filtered down to just that customer. ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey]) then removes any other filters on the Customer table while deliberately keeping the filter context transition just created on CustomerKey. SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) now sums only that one customer's sales, because the filter context -- via the relationship between Customer and Sales -- has narrowed the Sales table down to just their rows. Every row in the Customer table repeats this independently, one customer at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is exactly the kind of formula that looks impossible until you know about context transition, so I'd walk through it row by row. DAX is evaluating this calculated column for one specific customer at a time -- that's row context, nothing more. The moment CALCULATE appears inside that row context, DAX triggers context transition: it takes 'the row I'm currently on' and converts it into 'a filter restricting everything to just this row's CustomerKey.' ALLEXCEPT then does cleanup -- it strips any other filters that might be hanging around on the Customer table, while specifically preserving that CustomerKey filter context transition just created. So by the time SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) runs, the filter context has narrowed the related Sales table down to exactly one customer's transactions, through the relationship between the two tables. The IF then just compares that number to 2500. Nothing exotic is happening -- it's the standard shape of 'row context triggers CALCULATE triggers filter context,' which explains a whole category of DAX formulas that otherwise look like they're reading another table's data from inside row context by magic.
questions.example:
Customer Segment =
IF (
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( Sales[SalesAmount] ),
        ALLEXCEPT ( Customer, Customer[CustomerKey] )
    ) < 2500,
    "Low", "High"
)
-- CALCULATE triggers context transition: the current row's CustomerKey
-- becomes a one-value filter context, letting SUM reach into the related Sales table.
commonMistakes: Thinking a calculated column can never reference another table's aggregated data, missing that context transition is exactly what makes it possible
Forgetting that context transition happens automatically for an implicit CALCULATE wrapped around any measure reference, too
Misexplaining ALLEXCEPT as removing the CustomerKey filter instead of preserving it while removing everything else
Not recognizing the trigger condition precisely: CALCULATE evaluated inside row context
keyPoints: Context transition converts the current row context into an equivalent one-row filter context
It's triggered whenever CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside row context
A measure reference inside row context triggers it automatically too, via an implicit CALCULATE
ALLEXCEPT keeps the context-transition filter while removing other filters on the same table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines context transition and its trigger condition
Correctly walks through what happens for one customer row in this formula
Correctly explains ALLEXCEPT's role in preserving the context transition

questions.title: EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks
questions.prompt: You need to find every customer who has placed at least one order. Compare writing this with EXISTS, with IN, and with an INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT. Explain how each one behaves when a customer has multiple orders, and the specific trap with NOT IN when the subquery's column can contain NULLs.
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS, IN, and INNER JOIN with DISTINCT can all answer 'does this customer have at least one order,' but they get there differently. EXISTS(subquery) is a pure existence check -- SQL Server can stop scanning the moment it finds one matching row, and a customer with ten orders still only produces one result row, because EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's rows, just a true/false per outer row. IN (subquery) compares the outer column against the whole list the subquery returns; it also naturally avoids duplication since it's testing membership, not joining. An INNER JOIN behaves differently: joining Customer to Order on CustomerID and a customer with three orders produces three joined rows, which means DISTINCT (or GROUP BY) is required afterward to get back to one row per customer -- without it, the result silently overcounts. The sharper trap is with NOT IN rather than IN: if the subquery's column can contain a NULL, NOT IN against that list returns no rows at all for every single outer row, because SQL's three-valued logic can never prove an inequality against an unknown value. EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it's testing a condition, not comparing against a value list, which is one reason NOT EXISTS is generally the safer choice for 'does not have a match.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why these three roads to the same destination aren't actually equivalent in practice. EXISTS is the one I reach for by default for a pure existence check -- it's a yes/no test, the optimizer can bail out the instant it finds one match, and a customer with ten orders still contributes exactly one row to the result, because EXISTS never pulls the subquery's actual data back. IN behaves similarly for this particular case -- it's checking membership in a list, not joining, so it also doesn't duplicate. Where people get burned is reaching for a plain INNER JOIN instead: the moment you join Customer to Order, a customer with three orders becomes three rows, and if you forget the DISTINCT, you've silently inflated your result set without an error anywhere to tell you. But the real gotcha I always bring up, because it's bitten people in production, is NOT IN with a nullable column -- if even one NULL sneaks into the subquery's result, NOT IN returns completely empty, for every row, with no warning. I treat that as a hard rule: never write NOT IN against a column that could contain NULL -- use NOT EXISTS instead, which doesn't have that failure mode at all.
questions.example:
-- EXISTS: pure existence check, no duplication risk
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM [Order] o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

-- IN: membership test against the subquery's result list
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o);

-- JOIN: requires DISTINCT or a customer with 3 orders appears 3 times
SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
INNER JOIN [Order] o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;

-- THE TRAP: if Order.CustomerID can be NULL, this returns ZERO rows for every customer:
SELECT c.CustomerID FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o); -- avoid if nullable
commonMistakes: Writing a plain INNER JOIN for an existence check and forgetting DISTINCT, silently duplicating customers with multiple orders
Using NOT IN against a subquery column that can contain NULL, not realizing it returns zero rows for every outer row
Assuming EXISTS and IN always perform identically to a JOIN, when EXISTS can short-circuit and avoid materializing the whole list
Not recognizing that EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's column values -- only whether a match exists
keyPoints: EXISTS is a short-circuiting existence check; it returns one result row regardless of how many matches exist
IN compares against a list but doesn't duplicate rows the way a JOIN does
An INNER JOIN needs DISTINCT/GROUP BY to avoid duplicating a row per matching child record
NOT IN against a nullable column can return zero rows entirely -- NOT EXISTS avoids that trap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EXISTS's existence-check, non-duplicating behavior
Correctly explains why a JOIN needs DISTINCT to avoid duplication
Correctly identifies the NOT IN / NULL trap and why NOT EXISTS avoids it
Provides correct, illustrative SQL for at least two of the three approaches

questions.title: CTEs vs. Views: Same Shape, Different Lifetime
questions.prompt: A coworker says, "I don't get why we need views — a CTE already lets me name a subquery." Explain the real difference between a CTE and a view, and when you'd reach for one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE and a view can look nearly identical — both let you name a SELECT and reference it like a table — but they differ in lifetime and scope. A CTE, defined with WITH, exists only for the single statement immediately following it; the moment that statement finishes, the CTE is gone, and no other query, session, or user can reference it. A view, created with CREATE VIEW, is a permanent database object: it's saved once and can be queried by name from any session, any user with permission, indefinitely, until someone runs DROP VIEW. Neither one stores actual data — both re-run their underlying SELECT against live data every time they're referenced. The practical rule: reach for a CTE to make one complex query more readable, especially when you need to reference the same intermediate result twice in that query. Reach for a view when the same logic needs to be reused across many different queries, by many different people or tools, including reporting tools like Power BI connecting directly to the database.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the one-sentence version first: a CTE lives for one statement, a view lives forever until someone deletes it. If I'm writing a gnarly query with three levels of nested subqueries and I just want to name the middle layer so I can read my own logic back, that's a CTE — it's disposable, scoped to right here, right now. But if I've built a 'active customers with more than $1,000 in lifetime orders' query that three different reports are going to need, I don't want three copies of that logic drifting out of sync — I'd save it once as a view, under a clear name, so every query and every person on the team references the same definition. I'd also mention that a view is a real object other tools can see too — if Power BI is connecting directly to the database instead of importing through Power Query, it can query a view exactly like a table, which a CTE could never support.
questions.example:
-- CTE: scoped to this one statement only
WITH RecentOrders AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
    WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT * FROM RecentOrders WHERE Total > 5000;
-- RecentOrders no longer exists after this statement runs.

-- View: saved permanently, reusable by anyone with access
CREATE VIEW vw_RecentOrderTotals AS
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

SELECT * FROM vw_RecentOrderTotals WHERE Total > 5000;
commonMistakes: Assuming a CTE can be reused across multiple separate statements or sessions (it can't)
Assuming either one stores a physical copy of the data (both re-run their SELECT live)
Reaching for a view for a one-off readability fix inside a single complex query, when a CTE is simpler and doesn't leave a permanent object behind
Forgetting that a view is directly queryable by reporting tools connecting to the database, the way a CTE never could be
keyPoints: A CTE is scoped to one statement; a view persists until explicitly dropped
Neither stores data — both run their SELECT fresh against live data each time
CTEs suit one-off readability inside a single complex query
Views suit logic that needs to be reused across many queries, people, or tools

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains a CTE's one-statement lifetime
Correctly explains a view's persistent, reusable lifetime
States that neither stores data, both re-run live
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over the other

questions.title: What Makes a Window Function Different from GROUP BY
questions.prompt: Explain how a window function using OVER() differs from GROUP BY, and why you might reach for AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) instead of a GROUP BY query, even though both compute an average per category.
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY and a window function can compute the exact same aggregate — an average per category — but they do fundamentally different things to the result set. GROUP BY collapses every row in a group down into a single summary row, so a table of 500 products grouped by category becomes a handful of rows, one per category, with the individual products gone. A window function, triggered by adding OVER() to an aggregate, computes the same aggregate across a group of related rows but keeps every original row intact in the output — nothing collapses. PARTITION BY inside OVER() divides rows into groups purely for that calculation's purpose, exactly like GROUP BY divides rows, but the row-level result is untouched. The practical reason to reach for the window function version: you need the category average sitting alongside each individual product's own price, for example to compute how far above or below that category's average a specific product is priced — a comparison GROUP BY's collapsed output couldn't support at all, since the individual product's own price no longer exists in a grouped result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with what actually happens to the rows, because that's the real distinction, not just syntax. GROUP BY by category gives me one row per category — Bikes, Accessories, Clothing — and the individual products are gone from the output. AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) gives me back every single product row, but now each one also carries its own category's average price as an extra column sitting right next to it. That's the whole reason I'd reach for the window function version: I usually want to compare something at the row level against a group-level number — 'how does this specific product's price compare to the average for its category?' — and I can only do that math if both numbers are available on the same row. If all I actually need is the category averages themselves, with no individual rows attached, plain GROUP BY is simpler and I wouldn't bother with OVER() at all.
questions.example:
-- GROUP BY: collapses to one row per category
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
FROM Production.Product
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;

-- Window function: keeps every product row, adds the category average alongside it
SELECT Name, ProductSubcategoryID, ListPrice,
       AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS AvgPriceForCategory,
       ListPrice - AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS DiffFromAvg
FROM Production.Product;
commonMistakes: Saying GROUP BY and a window function always return the same number of rows (GROUP BY collapses; a window function does not)
Forgetting PARTITION BY is required to restart the calculation per group, not just ORDER BY
Assuming a window function requires an aggregate you can't also compute with GROUP BY — the aggregate itself is identical, only the row-collapsing behavior differs
Using GROUP BY when the goal was actually a row-level comparison against a group total, then wondering why the individual values disappeared
keyPoints: GROUP BY collapses rows into one summary row per group
A window function (OVER()) keeps every original row while still computing a per-group aggregate
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for the window calculation only, without collapsing anything
Choose the window function when you need a row-level value compared against a group-level aggregate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains GROUP BY's row-collapsing behavior
Correctly explains that a window function preserves every row
Correctly describes PARTITION BY's role
Gives a realistic scenario where the window function's row-level detail matters

questions.title: Measure or Calculated Column? The Decision Rule
questions.prompt: A new Power BI report builder asks you: "How do I know whether something should be a measure or a calculated column?" Give them a decision rule, and explain what actually goes wrong if they pick the wrong one.
questions.modelAnswer: The decision rule comes down to one question: do you need to slice, filter, or group by this value, or do you just need a summarized number to display? If the answer involves dragging something into a slicer, a legend, or the rows/axis of a visual, it has to be a calculated column, because only columns are filterable. If the answer is a total, ratio, or dynamically recalculated figure that should respond to whatever the report is currently filtered to, it has to be a measure. Picking wrong doesn't throw an error, which is exactly why it's dangerous. A calculated column computes once, at refresh time, in row context — if you use one where a measure belongs, the number silently freezes and stops responding the moment someone applies a filter or slicer, while looking perfectly plausible. A measure used where a column belongs simply can't be dragged into a slicer or an axis at all, because measures are evaluated in filter context and aren't filterable — Power BI just won't let you drop it there, which at least fails loudly rather than silently.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them to ask themselves one practical question before writing any DAX: 'Am I going to filter or group by this, or am I just going to look at it as a number?' If they're building a customer tier — High, Medium, Low — and they know they'll want to put that tier on a slicer or break out a table by it, that has to be a calculated column, because measures can't be dragged into a slicer at all. If they're building a percentage of total sales that should update the instant someone clicks a different region in a slicer, that's a measure, because only a measure re-evaluates live against whatever's currently filtered. The failure mode I'd really warn them about is the calculated column one, because it's the quiet one — it won't throw an error, it'll just sit there looking like a real number while actually being frozen at whatever it calculated the last time the model refreshed, and nobody notices until the totals stop making sense next to a working measure right beside it.
commonMistakes: Building a KPI or ratio as a calculated column, which freezes it at refresh time instead of letting it respond to report filters
Trying to build a filterable category as a measure, not realizing measures can't be dragged into a slicer or axis at all
Assuming the wrong choice always produces a visible error rather than a silently wrong number
Choosing based on which one 'looks easier to write' rather than whether the result needs to be filterable
keyPoints: The deciding question: filter/group by it, or just display a summarized number?
Calculated columns are filterable but frozen at refresh time (row context)
Measures are dynamic and recalculate per filter, but can't be used as a filter/slicer field themselves
Picking wrong fails silently for a calculated column, and fails loudly (can't drag it in) for a measure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the correct one-question decision rule
Correctly explains the silent-freeze failure mode of a wrong calculated column
Correctly explains the non-filterable limitation of a measure
Communicates it clearly enough for a newer report builder to actually apply

questions.title: FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE: Three LOD Keywords, Three Jobs
questions.prompt: Explain what a Level of Detail (LOD) expression is for in Tableau, and the real difference between the FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE keywords.
questions.modelAnswer: Every worksheet in Tableau normally computes at the level of detail implied by whatever dimensions sit on Rows, Columns, and the Marks card — that's the view's grain. An LOD expression lets a calculated field declare its own grain instead, independent of (or partially independent of) the view it's sitting in, which is necessary any time you need a number computed at a different level of detail than what's on screen, like a customer's lifetime total shown next to order-level rows. The three keywords control how the expression's scope relates to the view: FIXED computes at exactly the dimension(s) named in the braces, ignoring whatever else is on the view and most filters entirely. INCLUDE computes at the view's own dimensions plus whatever extra dimension is named, adding finer detail than the view would otherwise have. EXCLUDE computes at the view's dimensions minus whatever is named, removing detail the view would otherwise include. FIXED is the one used most often, but INCLUDE and EXCLUDE are specifically for calculations that need to stay partially tied to the view's own grain rather than being completely independent of it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the problem first, because the syntax doesn't make sense until the problem does: a worksheet grained by Order ID can't normally show you a customer's total lifetime sales next to each order, because a plain SUM(Sales) on that view only ever sums sales for that one order. FIXED solves that specific case — '{ FIXED [Customer Name] : SUM([Sales]) }' computes total sales per customer, full stop, no matter what's on the view, and that's the one I reach for probably 80% of the time I need an LOD. INCLUDE and EXCLUDE are for a narrower case: when I actually want the calculation to still track the view in some way, just with one dimension added or removed. A real example I'd give is a count of distinct products per order, shown on a view that's grained higher than order — INCLUDE [Order ID] lets that calculation drop down to the order level just for that one computation, while still respecting whatever else the view is sliced by.
questions.example:
{ FIXED [Customer Name] : SUM([Sales]) }       -- ignores the view and most filters entirely
{ INCLUDE [Order ID] : COUNTD([Product Name]) } -- view's grain + Order ID
{ EXCLUDE [Sub-Category] : SUM([Sales]) }        -- view's grain minus Sub-Category
commonMistakes: Assuming FIXED respects regular dimension filters the same way a plain aggregation would (it doesn't, unless the filter is promoted to a context filter)
Using FIXED when INCLUDE or EXCLUDE was actually needed, producing a number that's too independent of the view
Forgetting that an LOD expression computes before the view's own aggregation, not after it like a table calculation does
Treating all three keywords as interchangeable syntax rather than three genuinely different relationships to the view
keyPoints: LOD expressions let a calculation declare its own grain, independent of the view
FIXED computes at exactly the named dimension(s), ignoring the view and most filters
INCLUDE adds detail to the view's own grain; EXCLUDE removes detail from it
FIXED is the most commonly used keyword; INCLUDE/EXCLUDE matter when the calculation should stay partly tied to the view

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the problem LOD expressions solve
Correctly explains FIXED's behavior
Correctly distinguishes INCLUDE from EXCLUDE
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: LOD Expression or Table Calculation — When Does Each One Actually Run
questions.prompt: Both LOD expressions and table calculations in Tableau can compute something beyond the view's plain aggregation. Explain the real difference between them, specifically in terms of when each one runs in the query pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer: The distinguishing factor between an LOD expression and a table calculation isn't what either one can compute — it's when each one runs relative to the view's query. A regular aggregation like SUM(Sales) computes at the view's own grain with no special timing to consider. An LOD expression computes at a grain you name explicitly, and it runs before most filtering and before the view's own aggregation happens — it's part of the query Tableau sends to the data source. A table calculation runs after the view's query has already returned results; it only operates on the data that's already been aggregated and is sitting on screen, which is why a table calculation can reference things like 'the previous row' or 'rank within what's currently visible,' concepts that only make sense once a result set already exists. This has a real practical consequence: an LOD expression can see and compute against data that isn't currently displayed in the view (subject to FIXED's filter rules), while a table calculation is fundamentally limited to whatever rows the view already decided to show.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as 'before the plate arrives versus after it's already on the table.' An LOD expression is part of the actual query Tableau sends off to the database — it runs before the view's own aggregation, so it genuinely can touch data at a different grain than what's displayed, like a customer's full lifetime total even when the view itself is only showing this year's orders. A table calculation only gets to work with what's already come back and is sitting in the view — running totals, percent of total, rank — all of those only make sense as a second pass over data that already exists on screen. In practice this changes which one I reach for: if I need a number that depends on rows not currently visible in the view, that has to be an LOD expression, because a table calculation literally can't see outside what the view already pulled back.
commonMistakes: Assuming an LOD expression and a table calculation are interchangeable because both can produce a 'different grain' result
Trying to use a table calculation to reach data outside what the view has already returned (not possible — only an LOD expression can)
Forgetting that a table calculation depends on the view's layout (sort order, what's on Rows/Columns) in a way an LOD expression doesn't
Not recognizing that LOD expressions are computed as part of the query itself, while table calculations are a post-processing step
keyPoints: An LOD expression runs before the view's aggregation, as part of the query to the data source
A table calculation runs after the query returns, working only with what's already on screen
Only an LOD expression can reach data at a grain different from what the view currently displays
Table calculations suit things like running totals or rank that depend on the view's current layout

questions.title: VLOOKUP vs. XLOOKUP: More Than a Rename
questions.prompt: A colleague says XLOOKUP is "just VLOOKUP with a nicer name." Explain why that's wrong — what does XLOOKUP structurally fix that VLOOKUP cannot, even in principle?
questions.modelAnswer: XLOOKUP isn't a cosmetic rename — it fixes two structural problems VLOOKUP has by design, not just by convention. First, VLOOKUP's col_index_num argument is a hardcoded column position counted from the left edge of table_array; insert a new column anywhere inside that range and every existing VLOOKUP silently starts pulling from the wrong column, because the number is still a valid position, just no longer the right one. XLOOKUP replaces this with an independent return_array reference, so inserting a column elsewhere on the sheet can't shift what comes back. Second, and more fundamentally, VLOOKUP can only look to the right: the column you search by must be the leftmost column of table_array, because VLOOKUP's internal logic assumes that layout. XLOOKUP's lookup_array and return_array are two completely separate references, so it can look left just as naturally as right — searching by a value in column F and returning a value from column A is something VLOOKUP cannot do at all without physically rearranging the source data first, while XLOOKUP does it without any restructuring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently and give the one example that actually proves it's not just a rename: ask them to look up a Name and return the ID sitting in a column to its left. VLOOKUP genuinely cannot do that — not 'it's awkward,' but structurally cannot, because it only ever searches the leftmost column of whatever range you give it. XLOOKUP does it in one line, because lookup_array and return_array are just two independent ranges with no assumption about which one sits where. The other real fix, maybe more common in practice, is what happens when someone inserts a column into the middle of your lookup table — VLOOKUP's col_index_num is just a number, so it silently starts returning the wrong column's value with no error at all, while XLOOKUP's return_array is its own reference and isn't affected by a column being inserted elsewhere. Those are both genuine capability differences, not naming or syntax preferences.
questions.example:
=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])
-- Can ONLY look right; lookup column must be leftmost in table_array
-- col_index_num silently breaks if a column is inserted into table_array

=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found])
-- lookup_array and return_array are independent -- can look left or right
-- Immune to inserted columns, because return_array is its own reference
commonMistakes: Saying XLOOKUP is 'just VLOOKUP with better syntax' and missing the structural look-left capability
Forgetting VLOOKUP defaults to approximate match unless FALSE is explicitly passed as the 4th argument
Assuming XLOOKUP is always available (it requires Excel 365/2021+, not older installs)
Not recognizing that col_index_num's fragility to inserted columns is a design flaw, not just bad luck
keyPoints: VLOOKUP can only search the leftmost column of its range; XLOOKUP's two arrays are independent and can look either direction
VLOOKUP's col_index_num is a hardcoded position that breaks silently when a column is inserted
XLOOKUP's return_array is its own reference, immune to that same problem
These are structural differences, not just naming or convenience

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains VLOOKUP's leftmost-column limitation
Correctly explains XLOOKUP's independent-array fix
Correctly explains the inserted-column fragility of col_index_num
Makes clear these are structural, not cosmetic, differences

questions.title: Why a Spilled Array Is One Formula, Not Many
questions.prompt: Explain what makes a function like UNIQUE or FILTER a "dynamic array function," and why that matters compared to the legacy Ctrl+Shift+Enter array formulas Excel used before.
questions.modelAnswer: A dynamic array function returns as many values as its calculation produces, and if entered into a single cell, Excel automatically places the remaining results into the neighboring cells below and to the right — a behavior called spilling. Only the top-left cell of that spilled range actually holds the formula; every other cell inside the blue-bordered range shows the same formula, dimmed and non-editable, because it's a live result of that one formula, not independent cells. Before this engine existed, an equivalent calculation had to be entered as a legacy CSE array formula, confirmed with Ctrl+Shift+Enter instead of a plain Enter, and Excel wrapped it in curly braces automatically. The critical limitation of a legacy array formula is that its result size was fixed the moment it was entered — if the source data grew from 50 rows to 80, the formula didn't grow with it, and had to be manually reselected and re-entered. A dynamic array function resizes itself automatically every time the source data changes, with no re-entry required at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd demonstrate it rather than just describe it: type =UNIQUE(A2:A50) into one cell and press Enter, and watch Excel spill a whole deduplicated list down the column by itself, with a thin blue border drawn around the whole result. The thing worth calling out explicitly is that only that first cell actually holds the formula — click anywhere else inside that blue border and the formula bar shows the exact same formula, dimmed, not editable, because you're looking at one formula's live output, not five separate cells someone could individually overwrite. The old way, before this engine existed, meant pressing Ctrl+Shift+Enter instead of just Enter, and worse, locking in a fixed-size result the moment you did — add more rows to the source data next month and the old array formula just sits there, unchanged, until someone remembers to reselect the range and re-enter the whole thing. Dynamic arrays just resize themselves automatically, which is the actual improvement, not the keystroke.
questions.example:
Legacy (pre-2018, Ctrl+Shift+Enter):
{=SUM(IF(C2:C100="East",D2:D100))}
Fixed result size -- must reselect and re-enter if C2:C100 grows

Dynamic (Microsoft 365, press Enter):
=UNIQUE(C2:C100)
Spills automatically, resizes itself if C2:C100 grows
commonMistakes: Thinking a spilled range is five separate formulas rather than one formula with one editable cell
Trying to directly edit a cell inside the spilled range other than the top-left one
Assuming a legacy CSE array formula auto-resizes when source data grows (it doesn't)
Forgetting that a dynamic array function throws #CALC! if the spill range is blocked by existing data in the way
keyPoints: A dynamic array function spills its full result automatically into neighboring cells
Only the top-left cell of the spilled range holds the actual, editable formula
Legacy CSE array formulas were entered with Ctrl+Shift+Enter and had a fixed result size
Dynamic arrays resize themselves automatically when the source data changes; legacy ones require manual re-entry

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains spilling behavior
Correctly explains that only the top-left cell holds the formula
Correctly contrasts fixed-size legacy CSE formulas
States the practical benefit (auto-resize, no re-entry)

questions.title: fillna() or dropna(): Which One Is Actually Correct
questions.prompt: In pandas, both .fillna() and .dropna() deal with missing values, but neither is "more correct" in general. Explain how you'd decide which one to use for a given column of real data.
questions.modelAnswer: Neither .fillna() nor .dropna() is universally correct, because the right choice depends entirely on what a missing value actually means for that specific column, not on a general best practice. .dropna() removes any row with at least one missing value, which is appropriate when a missing value makes the entire row genuinely unusable for the analysis at hand — for example, a row missing its customer ID can't be meaningfully attributed to anyone, so keeping it around with a fake ID would be worse than dropping it. .fillna(value) replaces every missing value with a specific value instead, which is appropriate when a sensible default genuinely exists and is more informative than removing the row entirely — filling a missing Revenue column with 0 might be correct if a missing value there truly represents a $0 transaction, but incorrect if it actually represents 'we don't know the revenue for this sale,' since treating an unknown as a known zero will quietly understate every downstream total. The deciding step before writing either line of code is asking what the NaN itself represents for that column, not reaching for whichever function feels more common.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with the specific example I always use: a Revenue column with some NaN values. Before I write a single line of pandas, I ask what a missing Revenue actually means here — does it mean the sale genuinely had zero revenue, or does it mean we just don't have that data point for some other reason, like a failed data load? If it's genuinely zero, .fillna(0) is correct and actually more accurate than dropping the row, because the row is real, it just has a real value of zero. If it's 'we don't actually know,' filling it with zero is the worse choice, because now every SUM and AVG downstream quietly treats an unknown as a known number, and nobody looking at the final dashboard can tell the difference. In that second case I'd lean toward .dropna() for that specific analysis, or at minimum flag those rows separately so whoever reads the report knows some data was genuinely missing rather than legitimately zero.
questions.example:
df.isna().sum()          # count missing values per column first
df.fillna(0)              # use when a real default value exists
df.dropna()                # use when a missing value makes the row genuinely unusable
df.dropna(subset=["Revenue"])  # drop only rows missing in a specific column
commonMistakes: Defaulting to .fillna(0) for every numeric column without asking what a missing value actually represents
Defaulting to .dropna() without checking how many rows it would silently remove, which can shrink a dataset more than expected
Assuming one of the two functions is simply the 'more correct' or 'safer' default in general
Not running .isna().sum() first to understand how widespread the missing values actually are before deciding
keyPoints: Neither function is universally correct; the right choice depends on what NaN means for that column
.dropna() suits columns where a missing value makes the row genuinely unusable
.fillna(value) suits columns where a sensible, accurate default value actually exists
Filling an 'unknown' with a default like 0 can quietly distort downstream totals

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States that neither function is universally correct
Correctly explains when dropna() is appropriate
Correctly explains when fillna() is appropriate, and its risk
Frames the decision around what NaN means for that specific column

questions.title: Top-2-per-group with a window function
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns the two highest-priced products in each color, without using a correlated subquery.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic way to solve 'top N per group' in T-SQL is PARTITION BY plus ROW_NUMBER(), wrapped in a CTE so the ranking column can be filtered afterward. PARTITION BY Color restarts the numbering at 1 for each color, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC makes 1 the most expensive product in that color. You can't filter directly on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT's WHERE clause because window functions are logically evaluated after WHERE -- that's why the CTE (or a subquery) is necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'top N per group' problem, and the pattern I reach for every time is a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the grouping column. I avoid a correlated subquery with TOP 2 inside it because that approach re-executes once per outer row and doesn't scale well. Instead, I compute the rank once in a CTE, then just filter WHERE RankInColor <= 2 in the outer query. The one gotcha I always mention out loud in an interview: you cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2 directly in the same SELECT, because the WHERE clause is logically evaluated before window functions are computed -- that's exactly why the CTE wrapper is required, not just a style preference.
questions.example:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Color ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RankInColor
    FROM Production.Product
)
SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice
FROM Ranked
WHERE RankInColor <= 2
ORDER BY Color, RankInColor;
-- The CTE is required because ROW_NUMBER() can't be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
commonMistakes: Trying to filter WHERE ROW_NUMBER() <= 2 directly in the same SELECT (not legal -- window functions evaluate after WHERE)
Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table instead of per color
Using TOP 2 with a correlated subquery per group, which is correct but far less efficient on large tables
Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER(), which leaves 'top' undefined
keyPoints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per group (per color here)
A CTE or subquery is required to filter on the window function's result
ORDER BY DESC inside OVER() makes rank 1 the highest price
This pattern generalizes to any 'top N per group' business question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses ROW_NUMBER() with correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
Wraps it in a CTE/subquery to filter correctly
Query is syntactically valid and returns exactly 2 rows per color
Explains why filtering can't happen in the same SELECT's WHERE clause

questions.title: Temp table, table variable, or CTE?
questions.prompt: You need to hold an intermediate result set of about 500,000 rows, reuse it across three separate statements in a stored procedure, and would benefit from adding your own index to it. Which of #temp table, @table variable, or CTE would you choose, and why would the other two be worse choices here?
questions.modelAnswer: A #temp table is the right choice. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, so SQL Server maintains real statistics on it (row counts), which lets the optimizer build a much smarter plan for a large result set, and you can explicitly add your own indexes to it. A table variable would be the wrong choice here: it also lives in tempdb, but historically has no maintained statistics, so on older compatibility levels the optimizer may assume just one row and badly under-allocate resources for 500,000 rows -- and while you can add inline PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints, you can't add arbitrary indexes the way you can on a #temp table. A CTE would also be the wrong choice: it isn't physically stored at all -- it's inlined into the query -- so referencing it in three separate statements could mean SQL Server re-runs its underlying query multiple times, and you can't add an index to something that was never materialized.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given the three constraints in the question -- large row count, reused across multiple statements, and wanting an index -- a #temp table wins on all three. The decision rule I use: CTEs are for one-time readability or recursion, not for reuse -- a CTE doesn't store anything, it's re-inlined at every reference, so touching it from three separate statements risks the underlying query running three separate times. Table variables are for small result sets inside a procedure where I want to avoid plan recompiles -- but historically they carry no real statistics, so the optimizer can badly misjudge a large one. A #temp table is the one option that's physically stored with real statistics the optimizer can use, and the only one of the three where I can explicitly add an index after the fact. For 500,000 rows reused three times, I'm reaching for #temp every time.
commonMistakes: Choosing a CTE for something reused across multiple statements, not realizing it may re-run its query each time
Choosing a table variable for a large result set, assuming it always performs the same as a temp table
Not mentioning that #temp tables maintain real statistics while table variables historically don't
Forgetting that CTEs can't be indexed at all, since nothing is actually materialized
keyPoints: #Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and can be indexed
Table variables historically lack statistics, risking a poor plan on large sets
CTEs are inlined, not stored, and may re-execute their query on every reference
Choice depends on size, reuse, and whether an index is needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses the #temp table for this scenario
Correctly explains why a table variable would be worse here
Correctly explains why a CTE would be worse here
Provides valid, relevant example code

questions.title: Raising a custom business-rule error
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks whether a discount percentage exceeds 50% and, if so, raises a custom error using the modern recommended syntax. Then show how you would log an error inside a CATCH block and still let it propagate to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error, taking an error number, a message, and a state, and raising it exactly as if SQL Server had generated it itself. For a business rule like a discount cap, you check the condition and THROW a custom error if it's violated. To log an error and still propagate it, use THROW with no arguments inside a CATCH block -- it re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified, after whatever logging or cleanup logic runs first. RAISERROR is the older syntax, still common in existing code, with a different argument shape (message, severity, state) -- recognize it, but prefer THROW for new code.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the business rule check itself, I'd write a simple IF that tests the discount, and THROW a custom error number with a clear message if it's violated -- that's the modern, recommended way, and it's a one-liner. The more interesting half of this question is re-throwing from a CATCH block, because that's a pattern people often get wrong: they either swallow the error silently after logging it, or they try to reconstruct it with a new THROW statement and lose the original error details. The clean way is TRY/CATCH around the risky operation, log whatever you need to inside CATCH, and then just write THROW with no arguments -- that re-raises the exact error that was caught, unmodified, so the caller still sees the real failure instead of a sanitized stand-in.
questions.example:
-- Business rule check
IF @DiscountPercent > 50
    THROW 50000, 'Discount cannot exceed 50 percent.', 1;

-- Logging then re-throwing the original error
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Sales.SpecialOffer SET DiscountPct = @DiscountPercent WHERE SpecialOfferID = @ID;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (ErrorMessage, LoggedAt) VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), GETDATE());
    THROW; -- re-raises the exact caught error, unmodified
END CATCH
commonMistakes: Using RAISERROR for new code instead of the modern, recommended THROW
Writing a new THROW statement inside CATCH instead of bare THROW, which loses the original error's details
Forgetting THROW's argument order is (error number, message, state) -- a different shape than RAISERROR's
Swallowing the error entirely after logging it, instead of re-throwing so the caller knows it failed
keyPoints: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error
Bare THROW inside CATCH re-raises the exact original error
RAISERROR is the older syntax, still seen in legacy code
Logging an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses THROW to raise a custom business-rule error
Correctly uses TRY/CATCH with bare THROW to re-raise after logging
Explains the difference between THROW and RAISERROR

questions.title: Writing a percent-of-total measure
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure that shows each product category's sales as a percentage of total sales across the whole table, regardless of what category filter is currently applied on the report page.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic percent-of-total pattern, built with DIVIDE and REMOVEFILTERS. The numerator respects whatever's currently filtered (one category, if that's what's selected). The denominator wraps the same total-sales expression in CALCULATE with REMOVEFILTERS() as the filter argument, which strips away every active filter, giving the grand total across the entire table regardless of what's selected. Dividing the filtered numerator by the unfiltered denominator produces each row's share of the whole.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as two layers. First, I already have (or create) a plain Total Sales measure that just does SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) and naturally respects whatever filter context it's placed in -- one category if that's what the visual is sliced by. Then the percent-of-total measure wraps that same aggregation twice: once left alone as the numerator, and once inside CALCULATE with REMOVEFILTERS() as the denominator, which strips away every filter and gives me the grand total no matter what's selected. I always use DIVIDE instead of a plain '/' operator, specifically because DIVIDE handles a zero denominator gracefully instead of throwing a divide-by-zero error, which matters the moment someone filters down to a category with literally zero total sales in it.
questions.example:
%Sales =
DIVIDE(
    [Total Sales],
    CALCULATE([Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS())
)
-- Numerator respects the current filter (e.g. one category);
-- denominator strips all filters via REMOVEFILTERS(), giving the grand total.
-- DIVIDE avoids a divide-by-zero error if the filtered total is 0.
commonMistakes: Using a plain '/' operator instead of DIVIDE, risking a divide-by-zero error

Computing the denominator from a hardcoded total instead of dynamically removing filters, breaking if the data changes

The numerator is left as a plain measure so it respects the current filter context
DIVIDE is preferred over '/' because it handles a zero denominator gracefully
This pattern generalizes to any percent-of-total calculation

questions.title: Join Four Tables, Mixing INNER and LEFT
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012 that returns each order line's product name, order date, and the customer's first and last name, including order lines for products that may no longer have a subcategory assigned. Use at least one LEFT JOIN alongside INNER JOINs.
questions.modelAnswer: This requires chaining four tables together: SalesOrderHeader (for the order date and customer link), SalesOrderDetail (the order lines), Product (for the product name), and Person (for the customer's name), while also reaching ProductSubcategory with a LEFT JOIN so that products missing a subcategory still appear instead of being silently excluded. Each JOIN connects to whatever table already has the needed column available, not necessarily the very first table named in FROM — for instance, the join to Product uses ProductID from SalesOrderDetail, introduced by the join just before it. The LEFT JOIN to ProductSubcategory is the one deliberate choice: an INNER JOIN there would drop any order line whose product has a NULL ProductSubcategoryID, which is exactly the scenario the question asks to preserve.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this one join at a time rather than writing the whole thing at once, because that's the only way to keep four tables straight. I start from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail joined on SalesOrderID, since that's the backbone of the query. Then I bring in Product on ProductID to get the product name, and Person on CustomerID (really BusinessEntityID) to get the name. All three of those are INNER JOINs because I genuinely need a match on all of them for the row to make sense. The one place I'd stop and think is ProductSubcategory — the question specifically says some products might not have one, and an INNER JOIN there would quietly drop those order lines from the result with no warning. That's exactly the signal to use LEFT JOIN instead, so a product with a NULL ProductSubcategoryID still shows up, just with NULL in the subcategory column rather than vanishing from the report entirely.
questions.example:
SELECT soh.OrderDate, p.Name AS ProductName, per.FirstName, per.LastName, ps.Name AS SubcategoryName
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader AS soh
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON soh.SalesOrderID = sod.SalesOrderID
INNER JOIN Production.Product AS p
    ON sod.ProductID = p.ProductID
INNER JOIN Person.Person AS per
    ON soh.CustomerID = per.BusinessEntityID
LEFT JOIN Production.ProductSubcategory AS ps
    ON p.ProductSubcategoryID = ps.ProductSubcategoryID;
commonMistakes: Using INNER JOIN on ProductSubcategory, which silently drops any order line for a product missing a subcategory
Joining to the wrong table's column (e.g. trying to reach ProductID directly from SalesOrderHeader, which doesn't have it)
Forgetting table aliases on a four-table query, making it unreadable and error-prone to debug
Not noticing that CustomerID on SalesOrderHeader maps to BusinessEntityID on Person.Person, not a column literally named CustomerID there
keyPoints: Each JOIN can reference any table already available earlier in the query, not just the first one
LEFT JOIN preserves rows that would otherwise be dropped by a stricter INNER JOIN
Mixing INNER and LEFT JOIN in one query is normal when different relationships have different guarantees
Clear aliases are essential once a query joins more than two or three tables

Uses LEFT JOIN specifically for ProductSubcategory

questions.title: Building a FIXED LOD for Customer Lifetime Sales
questions.prompt: In Tableau, you need a calculated field that shows each customer's total lifetime sales, displayed correctly next to a view that's grained by individual order. Write the LOD expression and explain why a plain SUM(Sales) can't do this on an order-grained view.
questions.modelAnswer: The calculated field needs a FIXED LOD expression scoped to the customer dimension: { FIXED [Customer Name] : SUM([Sales]) }. On a view grained by Order ID, a plain SUM([Sales]) would compute only that one order's total, because a regular aggregation always computes at whatever grain the view currently has on Rows and Columns. FIXED breaks that dependency deliberately — it computes the aggregation at exactly the dimension named in the braces, Customer Name, regardless of what else is on the view. Dropped into a view with Order ID on Rows, every order line from the same customer shows the identical lifetime total next to it, which is exactly what makes it useful for comparing one order against that customer's overall relationship.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it as { FIXED [Customer Name] : SUM([Sales]) } and name it something like 'Customer Lifetime Sales.' The reason a plain SUM(Sales) can't do this comes down to what the view's own grain actually is — with Order ID on Rows, a regular SUM computes per order, full stop, because that's the level of detail Tableau's query is running at. FIXED exists specifically to break out of that: it tells Tableau to ignore whatever's on the view and compute the aggregation at exactly the dimension I name instead, so every single order row from the same customer repeats that customer's one lifetime number. I'd also flag the filter gotcha here, because it bites people constantly: if someone adds a regular Region filter expecting the lifetime total to shrink to just that region's sales, it won't, because FIXED ignores regular dimension filters by default — they'd have to promote that filter to a context filter first if they actually wanted FIXED to respect it.

Not testing the calculation against a view actually grained finer than the FIXED dimension, where the repeat behavior is visible

FIXED computes at exactly the named dimension, independent of the view
The result repeats identically across every row sharing that dimension's value

questions.title: Wiring a Filter Action from a Map to a Table
questions.prompt: You have a Tableau dashboard with a map of sales by state and a detail table of individual orders. Describe exactly how you'd configure a filter action so clicking a state on the map filters the table to just that state, and explain your trigger choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Configuring this requires opening Dashboard > Actions > Add Action > Filter, then setting the source sheet to the map and the target sheet to the detail table. The Run action on setting controls the trigger: Select is the correct choice here, because the action should fire only on a deliberate click, not on every mouse movement across the map. The dialog also asks what happens when the selection is cleared — clicking elsewhere on the dashboard to deselect the state — and the usual choice is to let the target revert to showing all data again rather than keeping its last filtered state, so the table doesn't get stuck showing one state after the user has moved on. Once saved, clicking any state on the map immediately narrows the table to that state's orders, and clicking empty space (or the same state again) clears the filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the exact dialog: Dashboard menu, Actions, Add Action, and pick Filter from the dropdown. Source sheet is the map, target sheet is the table. The setting I'd pay the most attention to is Run action on, and I'd deliberately pick Select rather than Hover. Hover is tempting because it feels more 'live,' but on a map with a lot of small states close together, Hover re-filters the table on every stray mouse movement, which reads as broken, not interactive — a viewer trying to read the table while their mouse happens to rest over a different state suddenly sees it change for no reason they intended. Select only fires on a genuine click, which matches what an actual viewer expects: 'I clicked a state, now show me that state's detail.' I'd also set 'on clear selection, show all values' so clicking away from the map resets the table instead of leaving it stuck on whatever was last selected.
commonMistakes: Choosing Hover as the trigger for a filter action, which re-filters on every incidental mouse movement
Forgetting to set the 'on clear selection' behavior, leaving the table stuck on a stale filter
Confusing a filter action with a highlight action -- a filter action removes data, it doesn't just dim it
Setting the target sheet incorrectly, filtering the map itself instead of the detail table

Source sheet triggers the action; target sheet receives the filter
Select is the correct trigger for a deliberate filter interaction, not Hover
The 'on clear selection' setting determines whether the target reverts or stays filtered
