questions.title: A VLOOKUP Broke When a Column Was Inserted — Fix It
questions.prompt: A workbook has =VLOOKUP(A2,ProductTable,4,FALSE) pulling a product's price. A coworker just inserted a new column into the middle of ProductTable, and now the formula returns the wrong value for every row with no error at all. Fix it so this can't happen again.
questions.modelAnswer: The formula is returning a wrong-but-plausible value because col_index_num is a hardcoded position counted from the left of ProductTable — when a new column was inserted, position 4 now points at a different column than the one that held Price before, and VLOOKUP has no way to know that happened, so it just returns whatever is currently sitting in that position without any error. The durable fix is to rewrite the lookup as an XLOOKUP, which replaces the positional argument with an independent reference to the actual Price column: =XLOOKUP(A2,ProductTable[ID],ProductTable[Price]). Because return_array now points at the Price column itself rather than a numeric position, inserting another column anywhere else in the table in the future can't silently shift what the formula returns — it will keep pointing at Price by name, not by position.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is actually confirm the diagnosis: check what's really in column 4 of ProductTable now versus what used to be there, and confirm the formula is returning that wrong column's value — not guessing, just looking. Once that's confirmed, the real fix isn't to just update the 4 to a 5 and move on, because the next time someone inserts a column, the exact same silent failure happens again. Instead I'd rewrite it as an XLOOKUP referencing the Price column directly: =XLOOKUP(A2,ProductTable[ID],ProductTable[Price]). If this is a proper Excel Table (which ProductTable's name suggests it might be), using structured references like that means the formula follows the actual Price column wherever it ends up, instead of trusting a number that has no idea the table's shape just changed. I'd also take two minutes to check every other VLOOKUP referencing this same table, because if one column insert broke this one, it almost certainly broke others too.
questions.example:
-- Before (fragile): breaks silently if a column is inserted into ProductTable
=VLOOKUP(A2,ProductTable,4,FALSE)

-- After (durable): return_array is its own reference to the Price column
=XLOOKUP(A2,ProductTable[ID],ProductTable[Price])
commonMistakes: Just changing the 4 to whatever the new correct position is, without fixing the underlying fragility
Not checking whether other formulas referencing the same table are also now returning wrong values
Forgetting to use structured table references, missing the chance to make the fix durable against future column inserts
Assuming the formula throwing no error means nothing is wrong, instead of recognizing a silent wrong answer as the real danger
keyPoints: col_index_num is a hardcoded position, not a reference to a named column
Inserting a column shifts that position silently, with no error raised
XLOOKUP's return_array is an independent reference, immune to that specific failure
The same underlying table likely has other VLOOKUPs with the identical fragile pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why the VLOOKUP returned a wrong value silently
Rewrites the formula as an XLOOKUP referencing the column directly
Explains why this fix prevents recurrence
Mentions checking for the same fragile pattern elsewhere

questions.title: One Formula: Filter, Then Sort, Then Spill
questions.prompt: Write a single Excel formula that returns only the rows from a sales table (columns A:D, data in rows 2-200) where the Region column (C) is "West", sorted by the Revenue column (D) descending, with no helper columns.
questions.modelAnswer: This requires nesting SORT around FILTER in a single formula: =SORT(FILTER(A2:D200,C2:C200="West"),4,-1). Read from the inside out, FILTER(A2:D200,C2:C200="West") first reduces the full range down to only the rows where the Region column equals "West", producing a dynamic array as its result. SORT then takes that filtered array directly as its own array argument, sorts it by its 4th column (Revenue, since FILTER's result still has the same column order as A:D), with a sort_order of -1 for descending. Because both functions are dynamic array functions, the whole expression spills automatically as one formula — no intermediate helper column or cell range is ever created on the sheet, and the result resizes itself automatically if the source data grows.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this from the inside out rather than trying to write the whole nested formula at once. First, just the filter piece on its own: =FILTER(A2:D200,C2:C200="West") — I'd actually type that alone first and confirm it spills the right rows before nesting anything else, since debugging a nested formula after the fact is much harder than confirming each layer works first. Once that's right, I wrap the whole thing in SORT: =SORT(FILTER(A2:D200,C2:C200="West"),4,-1). The second argument, 4, is the column to sort by inside the filtered result — and I'd double-check that's counting from FILTER's own output, not the original sheet's column D, which happens to line up here since Revenue genuinely is the 4th column of A:D. The -1 is just descending. One formula, no helper column, and if someone adds 50 more rows of sales data next month, it picks them up automatically.
questions.example:
=SORT(FILTER(A2:D200,C2:C200="West"),4,-1)
-- FILTER runs first: keeps only rows where Region = "West"
-- SORT then orders that filtered array by its 4th column (Revenue), descending
commonMistakes: Building this with a helper column and AutoFilter instead of one nested dynamic array formula
Using sort_index relative to the original sheet's columns instead of the filtered array's own column order
Forgetting the sort_order argument, which defaults to ascending (1), not descending
Not testing the FILTER portion alone first before nesting it inside SORT, making errors harder to isolate
keyPoints: FILTER runs first (innermost), reducing the range to matching rows
SORT then operates on FILTER's output directly, as one nested formula
sort_index refers to the position within the filtered array, not the original sheet
The whole expression spills automatically and resizes if source data grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes the correct nested FILTER/SORT formula
Correctly explains the inside-out evaluation order
Correctly specifies the sort column and descending order
Notes it's a single spilling formula with no helper columns

questions.title: Building a Margin % Calculated Field in a PivotTable
questions.prompt: You have a PivotTable with Profit and Revenue already in the Values area, broken out by Product Category. Add a Margin % field that's mathematically correct at every subtotal level, and explain why a plain average of row-level percentages wouldn't be.
questions.modelAnswer: The correct approach is a PivotTable calculated field, added from the Analyze (or PivotTable Analyze) tab's Calculations group, via Fields, Items & Sets > Calculated Field, with the formula Margin % = Profit/Revenue. A calculated field's formula operates on the aggregated totals of fields already in the PivotTable, not on individual rows, so Profit/Revenue at the Category subtotal level divides that category's summed Profit by that category's summed Revenue — a true ratio-of-sums, which is the mathematically correct way to compute a blended percentage. If instead you added a row-level Margin % column to the source data and then averaged it inside the PivotTable, each row's percentage would get equal weight in that average regardless of how large or small that row's actual revenue was, producing a number that doesn't represent the category's real blended margin at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open the PivotTable Analyze tab, go to Calculations, Fields Items & Sets, and pick Calculated Field. In the dialog, I'd name it Margin % and write the formula as Profit/Revenue, referencing the two fields that are already sitting in the PivotTable's Values area. The reason this works correctly at every subtotal level, and a row-level average wouldn't, comes down to what's actually being divided: this formula divides the summed Profit by the summed Revenue for whatever grouping you're looking at, which is the real, true blended margin for that category. If I'd instead built a per-row margin percentage on the source data and then averaged those percentages inside the PivotTable, a tiny row with a freakishly high margin would pull the average up just as much as a massive, representative row — the average has no idea that one row represents $50 of revenue and another represents $50,000. Ratio-of-sums avoids that distortion entirely.
questions.example:
Name:    Margin %
Formula: =Profit/Revenue
-- Added via: PivotTable Analyze tab > Calculations > Fields, Items & Sets > Calculated Field
commonMistakes: Building a row-level margin percentage column on the source data and averaging it inside the PivotTable
Not recognizing that a calculated field's formula operates on aggregated sums, not individual rows
Assuming Show Values As and a calculated field always produce the same result (they solve different problems)
Forgetting the calculated field only exists inside this one PivotTable, not as reusable source data
keyPoints: A calculated field's formula operates on the sums of fields already in the PivotTable
Margin % = Profit/Revenue computes a true ratio-of-sums at every subtotal level
Averaging row-level percentages gives every row equal weight regardless of its actual size
Ratio-of-sums is the mathematically correct way to represent a blended percentage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes how to add the calculated field
Writes the correct Margin % = Profit/Revenue formula
Correctly explains why ratio-of-sums is accurate at subtotal level
Correctly explains why averaging row-level percentages would be wrong

questions.title: Cleaning a Messy Sales DataFrame in Pandas
questions.prompt: You've loaded a CSV of sales data into a pandas DataFrame called df. It has some exact duplicate rows and some missing Revenue values. Write the pandas code to report how many of each problem exist, then remove the duplicates and fill missing Revenue with 0, explaining your reasoning for that specific fill choice.
questions.modelAnswer: The diagnostic step comes first: df.duplicated().sum() counts exact duplicate rows (excluding the first occurrence of each), and df['Revenue'].isna().sum() counts missing Revenue values specifically, giving a concrete sense of how bad each problem actually is before changing anything. df.drop_duplicates() then removes the duplicate rows, keeping the first occurrence of each. Filling Revenue specifically with 0, via df['Revenue'] = df['Revenue'].fillna(0), is only the right call if a missing Revenue value in this dataset genuinely represents a transaction with zero revenue (e.g. a free promotional item) rather than a transaction where the revenue is simply unknown or wasn't recorded — if it's the latter, filling with 0 would quietly understate every downstream total, and dropping those specific rows or flagging them separately would be more honest.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't touch the data until I know how bad each problem actually is, so the first two lines are purely diagnostic: df.duplicated().sum() tells me how many exact duplicate rows exist, and df['Revenue'].isna().sum() tells me how many rows are missing Revenue specifically. Once I've seen those numbers, I'd remove the duplicates with df.drop_duplicates() — straightforward, since an exact duplicate row is never legitimately two different sales. The Revenue fill is the part I'd actually think hardest about rather than just defaulting to fillna(0): I'd go find out, from whoever owns this data or from the data itself, whether a missing Revenue genuinely means the sale was free, or whether it means the field just didn't get recorded for some unrelated reason. If it's the first case, fillna(0) is accurate. If it's the second, filling with zero would make every total downstream quietly too low, and I'd rather flag those rows or drop them from revenue totals specifically than silently distort the number.
questions.example:
print(df.duplicated().sum())              # how many exact duplicate rows
print(df['Revenue'].isna().sum())          # how many missing Revenue values

df = df.drop_duplicates()
df['Revenue'] = df['Revenue'].fillna(0)    # only correct if NaN truly means $0, not "unknown"
commonMistakes: Filling missing Revenue with 0 reflexively without checking what a missing value actually represents
Dropping duplicates based on the whole row when the real duplicate definition should be narrower (e.g. a specific ID column)
Skipping the diagnostic count step and jumping straight to cleaning, with no record of how much data was affected
Not re-checking .duplicated().sum() after the fix to confirm the cleaning actually worked
keyPoints: Diagnose before cleaning: count duplicates and missing values separately
drop_duplicates() removes exact repeats, keeping the first occurrence
fillna(0) is only correct if missing genuinely means zero, not unknown
The fill choice should be justified by what the missing value represents, not applied automatically

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes correct diagnostic code for duplicates and missing values
Writes correct drop_duplicates() and fillna() code
Correctly reasons about when fillna(0) is and isn't appropriate here
Frames this as a judgment call, not a reflexive default

questions.title: Configuring a ForEach to Copy Multiple Tables
questions.prompt: In Azure Data Factory, you have an array variable TableList containing five table names. Describe how you'd configure a ForEach activity with a Copy activity inside it to copy each table, and explain your choice between running the iterations sequentially or in parallel.
questions.modelAnswer: The ForEach activity's Settings need the Items field pointed at the TableList array variable via Add dynamic content. Inside the ForEach, a Copy activity references the current iteration's value with @item() — for example, using @item() as the source table name in the Copy activity's source dataset parameters, so each pass through the loop copies a different table named by whatever TableList currently holds at that position. The sequential-vs-parallel decision depends on whether the five copies are genuinely independent of each other: if each table writes to its own separate destination file or table with no shared resource between iterations, running in parallel (isSequential: false) with a reasonable batchCount is safe and faster. If any iterations could write to the same destination, or depend on state created by an earlier iteration, isSequential: true is the safer choice, even though it's slower, because parallel iterations sharing a destination can produce a genuine write conflict.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set up the ForEach's Items field to point at the TableList variable through Add dynamic content, then drop a Copy activity inside the loop body. Inside that Copy activity's source configuration, I'd reference @item() as the table name, so on the first pass it's whichever table is first in the array, and so on through all five. The real decision I'd actually stop and think about is sequential versus parallel. If these five tables are each landing in their own separate destination — five different files, or five different target tables — I'd run it in parallel, because there's no shared resource between iterations and it'll finish in a fraction of the time. But if, for some reason, more than one of these copies could end up writing to the same destination file or the same staging table, I'd force isSequential to true even though it's slower, because two parallel iterations racing to write the same file is exactly the kind of bug that's hard to reproduce and worse to debug after the fact.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a single table name instead of referencing @item() inside the loop
Defaulting to parallel execution without checking whether iterations share a destination resource
Forgetting the 100,000-item limit and 50 max batchCount for parallel ForEach runs
Trying to nest a second ForEach directly inside this one instead of using an Execute Pipeline activity
keyPoints: Items is set via dynamic content referencing the array variable
@item() inside the loop references the current iteration's value
Parallel execution is safe only when iterations don't share a destination or resource
Sequential is the safer default whenever iterations aren't genuinely independent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes configuring the ForEach's Items field
Correctly describes using @item() inside the Copy activity
Makes a reasoned sequential-vs-parallel decision
Explains the write-conflict risk of parallel execution

questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution
Proposes consistent table access order as a concrete fix
Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows
Provides a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Rewrite correctly handles the full year's date range without off-by-one errors

questions.title: A measure is ignoring the report's slicer selections
questions.prompt: A measure called 'West Region Sales' was written as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), Geography[Region] = "West"). When a user applies a slicer on Geography[State] set to multiple East Coast states, the measure still shows West region totals instead of narrowing further. Explain why, and how you'd fix it if the intent is for the measure to respect both the hardcoded region condition and the slicer together.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a column mismatch, not a CALCULATE overwrite problem in the way it first appears -- the measure filters Geography[Region], while the slicer filters Geography[State], a different column entirely, so there's nothing for CALCULATE to overwrite; the measure's filter on Region and the slicer's filter on State both remain active simultaneously, and the combination (West region AND East Coast states) likely returns an empty or near-empty result, which can look like the measure is 'ignoring' the slicer when it's actually honoring an impossible intersection. The real fix depends on intent: if Region and State should interact at all, the model likely needs the measure's logic reconsidered -- for instance, if the actual intent was ever for CALCULATE to override a same-column filter, KEEPFILTERS would make a new filter combine with (intersect) an existing one on the same column instead of overwriting it, but that only applies when both filters target the same column, which isn't the case here. The practical fix is recognizing the filters are on different columns and adjusting the DAX to filter on the column that's actually meant to interact with the slicer, or removing the hardcoded Region condition if State should be the only filter that matters.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether the measure's filter and the slicer's filter are even on the same column, because that's the detail that changes the whole diagnosis. Here they're not -- the measure hardcodes Geography[Region] = "West", and the slicer is on Geography[State]. CALCULATE's overwrite-by-default behavior only kicks in when a new filter targets a column that's already filtered; since Region and State are different columns, both filters stay active at the same time, which means the measure is actually doing exactly what it's coded to do -- show West region sales, further restricted to whichever East Coast states happen to also be in the West region (probably none, hence a confusing near-empty or unexpected result). This is a case where I'd go back to the business requirement rather than reach for KEEPFILTERS, because KEEPFILTERS solves same-column conflicts, and this isn't one. If the real intent was for the slicer to be the only thing controlling region/state filtering, I'd remove the hardcoded Region condition from the measure entirely rather than trying to patch the filter interaction.
questions.example:
-- The problem: two different columns filtered simultaneously, not a same-column overwrite
West Region Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), Geography[Region] = "West")
-- Slicer filters Geography[State] (East Coast states) -- a different column,
-- so both filters stay active together, likely producing an empty intersection.

-- If the true intent is for the slicer alone to control the result:
Region Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) -- no hardcoded CALCULATE filter at all
commonMistakes: Assuming the measure 'isn't respecting' the slicer because of CALCULATE's overwrite behavior, when the real issue is two different columns both staying active
Reaching for KEEPFILTERS as a fix without checking whether the two filters even target the same column
Not recognizing that an unexpected near-empty result can be the system behaving correctly against a flawed assumption
Fixing the symptom by changing the slicer instead of questioning whether the hardcoded Region filter belongs in the measure at all
keyPoints: CALCULATE's overwrite-vs-combine behavior only applies to filters on the same column
A measure filtering one column and a slicer filtering a different column both stay active together
An unexpected result can mean the filters are correctly combining into an impossible intersection
The fix should match actual business intent, not just reflexively apply KEEPFILTERS or REMOVEFILTERS

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that Region and State are different columns, both staying active
Correctly explains why this isn't a CALCULATE overwrite scenario
Proposes a fix grounded in actual business intent rather than a reflexive KEEPFILTERS/REMOVEFILTERS patch

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)
Explains what to check before killing the blocking session
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SELECT * as the likely cause
Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns
Notes the fix depends on the index already covering those exact columns

questions.title: A Count by Employee Shows the Same Number for Every Project
questions.prompt: In a Power BI model with CompanyProject, ProjectHours, and CompanyEmployee tables (ProjectHours in the middle, related to both), a visual counting distinct employees per project shows the identical number repeated for every project instead of varying counts. What's the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The likely cause is that the relationship between ProjectHours and CompanyEmployee is set to Single cross-filter direction, so filtering by CompanyProject reaches ProjectHours but doesn't continue through to CompanyEmployee — the employee count effectively ignores which project is selected and counts across the whole employee table every time, producing the same repeated number. The fix is to change that relationship's cross filter direction to Both, letting a filter from CompanyProject travel all the way through ProjectHours to CompanyEmployee. This works cleanly here because it's a simple star shape with ProjectHours in the center; if changing it to Both causes Power BI to reject the relationship or warn about ambiguity, that signals a loop elsewhere in the model (for instance, another path connecting CompanyProject and CompanyEmployee), which would need to be resolved separately, typically by marking one relationship inactive.
questions.professionalAnswer: The symptom — identical repeated numbers instead of varying ones — is the classic signature of a filter not actually reaching the table being counted, so that's where I'd look first, not at the DAX itself. I'd open Manage relationships and check the cross filter direction on the ProjectHours-to-CompanyEmployee relationship specifically, since that's the one standing between the project filter and the employee count. If it's set to Single, that's almost certainly it: a filter from CompanyProject reaches ProjectHours fine, but Single direction stops it from continuing on to CompanyEmployee, so the count of distinct employees just ignores the project filter entirely and returns the same whole-table number every time. Switching that relationship to Both should fix it immediately in a simple star-shaped model like this. If Power BI pushes back and won't let me set it to Both, or warns about ambiguous filtering, that tells me there's a second path connecting those two tables somewhere I haven't accounted for, and I'd need to find and break that loop before Both can safely apply.
commonMistakes: Assuming the DAX formula itself is wrong before checking the relationship's cross filter direction
Setting every relationship in the model to Both without checking for loops first, which can cause Power BI to reject the change
Not recognizing the 'identical repeated number' symptom as specifically a filter-not-reaching-the-table problem
Fixing this one relationship without checking whether other visuals in the report rely on the Single-direction behavior elsewhere
keyPoints: Single cross filter direction stops a filter from reaching past the immediate related table
The 'same number repeated everywhere' symptom indicates the filter isn't reaching the counted table at all
Both direction lets a filter in a simple star schema travel all the way through
A model with loops may reject Both and need an inactive relationship instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies cross filter direction as the likely cause
Correctly explains why Single direction produces this exact symptom
Provides the correct fix (switch to Both)
Mentions the loop/ambiguity caveat

questions.title: A Scheduled Refresh Quietly Stopped Running
questions.prompt: A Power BI semantic model's scheduled refresh hasn't actually updated the data in over a week, but nobody got an obvious single alert about it being "turned off." What's the most likely explanation, and what are the two things you'd check first?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is Power BI's four-failures rule: after four consecutive scheduled refresh failures, Power BI automatically disables the schedule, with no prominent standing banner beyond the failure emails that were sent at the time, which are easy to miss or filter out. The two things to check first are the gateway, since an outdated gateway version is behind a surprising number of otherwise-confusing refresh failures, and whether the report has a gateway selected at all, since the underlying data source may have changed or gone missing. After identifying and fixing the underlying cause — commonly expired credentials — re-enabling requires going back to Schedule refresh and manually flipping the toggle back on; simply fixing the root cause doesn't automatically turn a disabled schedule back on.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 'quietly stopped, no obvious single alert' detail is the real clue here, and it points straight at the four-failures rule: Power BI automatically disables a scheduled refresh after four consecutive failures, and the only trace of that is the failure emails that went out at the time, which are genuinely easy to miss, especially if the original owner isn't checking that inbox closely. Before I go hunting for anything exotic, the two things I'd check first are the basics the official troubleshooting guidance always starts with: is the gateway up to date, since an outdated gateway causes a surprising share of failures that look unrelated on the surface, and does this report even have a gateway selected right now, since a changed or removed data source would also silently break things. Once I find and fix whatever actually caused the failures — expired credentials being the most common culprit — I'd remember that fixing the cause alone doesn't turn the schedule back on; I have to go back into Schedule refresh and flip it on myself.
commonMistakes: Assuming a single obvious error or notification caused this, rather than the quiet four-failures auto-disable
Fixing the root cause (e.g. expired credentials) and assuming the schedule resumes automatically, without re-enabling it
Skipping the gateway-version check as 'too basic' before diagnosing something more complex
Not checking refresh history for the actual error message, which usually names the specific failure directly
keyPoints: Four consecutive failures auto-disable a scheduled refresh with no prominent standing alert
Check gateway version and whether a gateway is selected at all, before anything more exotic
Refresh history logs every attempt's status and error message
Fixing the cause doesn't re-enable the schedule -- that toggle must be flipped back on manually

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the four-failures auto-disable as the likely cause
Names the two basic checks (gateway version, gateway selected)
Notes refresh history as where to find the actual error
States that the schedule must be manually re-enabled after the fix

questions.title: Joining Orders to a Summary Table Doubled the Shipping Total
questions.prompt: A Tableau workbook joins an Orders table (one row per line item) to an Order Summary table (one row per order, with a flat ShippingFee column) on Order ID. The SUM of ShippingFee in the resulting view is much higher than it should be. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a classic fan-out: Orders has multiple rows per Order ID (one per line item) while Order Summary has exactly one, so joining them duplicates each Order Summary row once for every line item that order has. ShippingFee, a value that genuinely belongs once per order, gets repeated across every duplicated row, and summing it then adds that same flat fee multiple times for any order with more than one line item — the more line items an order has, the more inflated its contribution to the total becomes, while every individual row still looks completely correct on its own. The fix is to avoid combining these two different grains with a row-level join at all: using a relationship instead (which aggregates each side to the worksheet's actual needed grain rather than combining rows immediately) sidesteps the problem, or, if a join is unavoidable, computing the shipping total at the order level first — via an LOD expression like { FIXED [Order ID] : MAX([ShippingFee]) }, or by pre-aggregating before the join — avoids summing a duplicated value.
questions.professionalAnswer: The inflated total with every individual row still looking correct is the signature of a fan-out, so that's what I'd check first: are these two tables actually at the same grain? They're not here — Orders is one row per line item, Order Summary is one row per order — and joining them on Order ID duplicates every Order Summary row once for each line item in that order. ShippingFee is an order-level value, so when it gets duplicated across, say, four line-item rows for one order, summing it adds that one $15 shipping fee four times instead of once, and the more items an order has, the worse the overcount gets. The real fix is to stop combining these at the row level entirely — if I switch from a join to a relationship, Tableau aggregates each side to whatever grain the worksheet actually needs instead of multiplying rows up front, which avoids this specific problem by design. If a join genuinely has to stay, I'd wrap ShippingFee in a FIXED LOD on Order ID so it's computed once per order regardless of how many line-item rows got joined in alongside it.
commonMistakes: Assuming every individual row's ShippingFee value must be wrong, when actually each row is correct and only the SUM is inflated
Not checking whether the two tables share the same grain before joining them
Switching to a relationship without confirming it actually resolves this specific aggregation, rather than just assuming it does
Trying to fix the SUM by filtering rows instead of addressing the underlying grain mismatch
keyPoints: A fan-out happens when joining tables of mismatched granularity
Order-level values get duplicated and over-summed once per matching line-item row
Individual rows look correct; only the aggregate is wrong
A relationship, or an LOD expression fixed to Order ID, avoids summing the duplicated value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the fan-out / granularity mismatch
Correctly explains why individual rows look right but the SUM is wrong
Proposes a correct fix (relationship or FIXED LOD)
Notes that this is specifically an aggregate-level problem, not a row-level one

questions.title: A Dashboard "Feels Slow" — What Do You Actually Do First
questions.prompt: A stakeholder says a Tableau dashboard "feels slow" and asks you to speed it up. Before changing anything, what's your first step, and how do you use it to figure out what's actually worth fixing?
questions.modelAnswer: "Feels slow" is not a diagnosis, so the first step is to record a Performance Recording (Help > Settings and Performance > Start Performance Recording in Tableau Desktop), interact with the dashboard the way a real user would — opening it, applying filters, switching sheets — then stop the recording, which opens a new workbook holding the results. The Events view, sorted by duration, shows exactly which recorded event took the longest, by name, with an actual duration attached — Generating Extract, Executing Query, Geocoding, Computing Layout, and so on — turning a vague impression into a specific, falsifiable finding like "Executing Query took 4.2 seconds and everything else was under 0.3 seconds." Whatever category shows up at the top of that list is where optimization effort should go first, and the fix should be verified by recording again afterward to confirm the specific bottleneck actually improved, rather than just assuming a change helped.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch anything, I'd actually record what's happening rather than guessing based on a feeling, because 'feels slow' could mean a dozen different things and guessing wastes everyone's time trying things that might not even be the real problem. I'd start a Performance Recording, click through the dashboard the way the stakeholder actually uses it — open it, apply a filter or two, switch between sheets — then stop the recording and open the resulting workbook. The Events view is where I'd look first, because it sorts every recorded step by how long it actually took, longest first, so instead of guessing I get something concrete like 'Executing Query took 4.2 seconds, nothing else even got close.' That tells me exactly where to spend my time — if it's a slow query, I'm looking at the data source or the calculations driving that query, not randomly simplifying a chart that was never the actual bottleneck. And after I make a change, I'd record again to confirm that specific number actually improved, instead of just assuming it did because the dashboard felt faster to me personally.
commonMistakes: Trying things (simplifying a filter, turning off a calculation) before recording what's actually slow
Treating 'it feels faster now' as proof of improvement instead of re-recording to confirm
Looking only at the Timeline view and missing the Events view's sorted-by-duration ranking
Assuming the fix for one workbook's bottleneck (e.g. extract generation) applies universally to every slow dashboard
keyPoints: "Feels slow" is not a diagnosis -- measure before optimizing
Performance Recording captures named, timed events during real interaction
The Events view sorts by duration, surfacing the actual bottleneck directly
Re-recording after a fix confirms whether it actually helped

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies Performance Recording as the correct first step
Correctly describes how to use the Events view to find the bottleneck
Explains why guessing/trying things first is the wrong approach
Mentions re-recording after a fix to verify improvement

questions.title: A Power Query Refresh Broke After the Source File Changed
questions.prompt: An Excel workbook's Power Query import ran fine for months, pulling from a weekly CSV export. After the source system changed its export slightly, refreshing the query now throws type-mismatch or column-not-found errors. What's the most likely cause, and how would you make the query more resilient?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that Power Query steps reference columns by name and position in a way that's brittle to upstream changes — a renamed column, a reordered column, or a column whose underlying values now include something the locked-in data type can't represent (for example, a numeric column that now sometimes contains a text value) will break a query that was built assuming the export's shape would never change. Each Applied Step in Power Query runs in order and depends on the previous step's output matching what it expects, so a change upstream of where a step currently operates (a reordered column, a renamed one) can invalidate that step outright. Making the query more resilient means checking Applied Steps for exactly where the break occurs, re-pointing any step that referenced the old column name or position, and reconsidering overly specific type changes early in the query if the source's column order or exact naming is known to shift periodically — sometimes restructuring to select columns by name rather than position avoids the fragility entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd do is open the query in Power Query Editor and look at Applied Steps, because that list tells me exactly which step is now failing, rather than guessing at the whole query. Power Query steps run top to bottom, each one assuming the previous step's output looks a certain way, so if the source system renamed a column or changed its position, whichever step first references that column by its old name or position is going to be the one that breaks — and that error message, however cryptic it looks ('type mismatch,' 'column not found'), is usually pointing right at that spot once I check Applied Steps in order. Once I find it, the fix is usually just re-pointing that step to the new column name, or adjusting the type-change step if a column that used to be clean numbers is now occasionally getting a text value mixed in. If this source is known to shift its export format periodically, I'd also think about whether a step is relying on column position instead of column name, and change it to be more robust against future reordering, since that's the exact fragility that caused this specific break.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the entire query from scratch instead of checking Applied Steps for where it actually broke
Assuming the error is random or a one-off glitch, rather than tracing it to a specific upstream schema change
Fixing the immediate error without checking whether other steps downstream rely on the same now-changed column
Not considering whether a step depends on column position rather than column name, missing a chance to make it more durable
keyPoints: Applied Steps run top to bottom, each depending on the previous step's shape
A renamed, reordered, or retyped source column can break whichever step first references it
Checking Applied Steps in order usually pinpoints exactly where the break occurred
Referencing columns by name rather than position makes a query more resilient to future source changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies a source schema change as the likely cause
Correctly describes using Applied Steps to locate the break
Proposes a concrete fix for the immediate error
Proposes a way to make the query more resilient going forward
