questions.title: The Pipeline Shows "Succeeded" Even Though a Copy Activity Failed
questions.prompt: An Azure Data Factory pipeline has a Copy activity whose Upon Failure path connects to a cleanup activity. Last night the Copy activity genuinely failed, the cleanup ran successfully, and the pipeline's overall run status still shows "Succeeded." Is this a bug? Explain what's actually happening and how you'd change the design if you want a failed Copy to make the whole pipeline show red.
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a bug — it's the Try-Catch pattern behaving exactly as designed. Data Factory determines overall pipeline status only by looking at leaf activities, the ones with nothing connected downstream of them. Here, only Upon Failure is defined from the Copy activity, routing to the cleanup activity; there's no Upon Success or Upon Skip path defined from the Copy activity itself feeding into anything else, so the cleanup activity (which succeeded) is the only leaf activity Data Factory evaluates, and a successful leaf means the pipeline reports Succeeded — the Copy activity's own failure is absorbed rather than surfaced. To make a failed Copy actually show red at the pipeline level, switch to a Do-If-Else pattern: define both an Upon Failure path (to the cleanup/error handler) and an Upon Success path from the Copy activity, each leading to further downstream activities — with both paths now feeding leaf activities, a failure on the Copy activity side becomes a failure on a leaf activity, and the overall pipeline status reports Failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them it's genuinely not a bug, even though I understand why it looks like one at first glance — this is Try-Catch doing exactly what it's designed to do. The key detail is that Data Factory only looks at leaf activities — the ones with nothing after them — to decide whether the whole pipeline succeeded or failed. In this design, the only thing defined after the Copy activity is its Upon Failure path into the cleanup activity, so when the cleanup activity finishes successfully, that's the only leaf activity in the picture, and a successful leaf means a successful pipeline, full stop — the Copy activity's own failure never gets to 'vote' on the overall status because nothing is watching for it at the top level. If they want a failed Copy activity to actually make the pipeline go red — say, so a downstream alert fires — the fix is to switch to Do-If-Else: define both an Upon Failure and an Upon Success path out of the Copy activity, each leading somewhere, so now both outcomes are being tracked as leaf-level paths instead of only the failure path being absorbed by the handler.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is a bug in Data Factory rather than the designed behavior of leaf-activity status evaluation
Confusing the Try-Catch pattern (absorbs failure, reports success) with Do-If-Else (surfaces failure)
Not recognizing that only leaf activities (nothing downstream) determine overall pipeline status
Trying to fix this by adding more logging inside the cleanup activity instead of restructuring the activity paths
keyPoints: Pipeline status is determined only by leaf activities -- ones with nothing downstream
Try-Catch (only Upon Failure defined) absorbs the failure and reports overall success
Do-If-Else (both Upon Failure and Upon Success defined) surfaces the failure to the pipeline level
This is intended behavior, not a bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains this is intended Try-Catch behavior, not a bug
Correctly explains the leaf-activity status evaluation rule
Proposes the correct Do-If-Else fix
Explains why Do-If-Else changes the outcome

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered vs. nonclustered distinction
Correctly lists the three traits of a good clustering key
Applies the tradeoff to the specific nightly-load scenario given
Recommends a nonclustered index to support the ProductID range queries

questions.title: Bridge table or a direct many-to-many relationship?
questions.prompt: Power BI allows a direct many-to-many relationship between two tables without building a bridge table yourself. Given that, explain when you'd still choose to build an explicit bridge table for a Sale-to-Salesperson relationship instead of just setting the relationship's cardinality to many-to-many directly.
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI's direct many-to-many relationship setting is convenient -- it lets two tables relate without an intermediate table, and Power BI handles the filtering internally. But it comes with real tradeoffs: it can be harder to reason about and debug when filter results look wrong, and it doesn't give you anywhere to attach additional information about the relationship itself -- a role, a credit percentage, a date the association started. An explicit bridge table is still the better choice whenever any of those matter: if a salesperson's credit on a sale isn't always equal (say, a 60/40 split between two reps), the bridge table is exactly where that percentage lives, as a real column -- a direct many-to-many relationship setting has no equivalent. A bridge table is also more transparent during debugging: you can literally query it and see the actual association rows, whereas a direct many-to-many relationship's behavior is more opaque. I'd default to a direct many-to-many relationship for a quick, simple case with no extra attributes needed, and build an explicit bridge table the moment the relationship itself needs to carry data or the model needs to be debuggable by someone besides me.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the direct many-to-many setting as the quick path, and the bridge table as the path I take once the relationship itself needs to say more than just 'these two things are associated.' If all I need is 'this sale involved these salespeople,' with nothing else attached to that fact, the built-in many-to-many relationship setting is genuinely fine and saves me a table. But the moment the relationship needs its own data -- like a credit split percentage when a sale is shared 60/40 between two reps, or a 'role' on the sale like 'lead' vs. 'support' -- there's no column to put that on if I'm just flipping a cardinality setting; a bridge table, by contrast, is just a regular table, so I add CreditPercent or Role as columns on it without a second thought. I'd also reach for an explicit bridge table on anything a teammate besides me will need to maintain or debug, because 'query the bridge table and look at the rows' is a much easier thing to hand off than 'understand how Power BI's internal many-to-many filtering works.' So my actual rule is: default to the built-in setting for a quick, attribute-free case, and build the bridge table the moment the relationship needs to carry its own information or needs to be transparent to someone else on the team.
commonMistakes: Treating the built-in many-to-many setting and a bridge table as functionally identical in every case
Missing that a bridge table can hold its own attributes (credit percentage, role) while a direct relationship setting cannot
Defaulting to a bridge table every time without considering the simpler built-in setting is sufficient for a bare association
Not considering debuggability/maintainability by other teammates as a real factor in the decision
keyPoints: Power BI's direct many-to-many relationship setting handles a bare association without an extra table
A bridge table is still preferred when the relationship itself needs to carry attributes (credit %, role, date)
A bridge table is more transparent to query and debug than the internal behavior of a direct many-to-many relationship
The decision should be based on whether the relationship needs its own data, not just convenience

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what the built-in many-to-many relationship setting does
Correctly identifies that a bridge table can carry its own attributes and the direct setting can't
Correctly identifies debuggability/transparency as a reason to prefer a bridge table
Gives a clear, sensible decision rule

questions.title: Views, or Raw Tables, as the Layer Power BI Connects To
questions.prompt: You're setting up a new Power BI semantic model that will query SQL Server directly. A teammate suggests pointing Power BI straight at the base tables. Would you recommend that, or a layer of views in between? Justify your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: A layer of views between the base tables and Power BI is generally the better design, for reasons that go beyond simple convenience. A view lets the BI layer depend on a stable, named contract — SELECT CustomerID, FirstName, LastName FROM dbo.vw_Customers — instead of depending directly on base table structure that database developers may need to change for unrelated reasons (renaming a column, splitting a table, adjusting a join elsewhere in the schema). As long as the view's output columns stay the same, the underlying tables can evolve without breaking the Power BI model at all. Views also let the database team pre-bake business logic once — a consistent definition of "active customer," a standard join eliminating duplicate rows — so every report built on top of vw_ActiveCustomers uses the identical, tested definition instead of each report author re-deriving (and potentially getting slightly wrong) the same logic independently. The tradeoff is an extra layer to maintain and document, and views add no meaningful performance cost since they're just saved SELECT statements executed live.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recommend views, and the argument I'd actually make is about who owns the risk of changing the schema later. If Power BI points straight at base tables, any future change to those tables — even one that has nothing to do with reporting, like a database developer normalizing a column for an unrelated application feature — risks silently breaking the semantic model, because Power BI now depends on the table's exact current shape. A view sits in between as a stable contract: as long as vw_Customers keeps returning the same columns, the tables underneath it can be restructured freely without Power BI ever noticing. The second reason I'd give, maybe even more practical day to day, is that a view lets us define business logic once instead of every report builder re-deriving it slightly differently — one agreed, tested view of 'active customer' or 'current fiscal year sales,' instead of five dashboards each quietly defining it a little differently. The cost is one more layer to maintain, but for a model that's going to be queried repeatedly by BI tools, that cost is worth paying.
commonMistakes: Pointing Power BI directly at base tables, coupling the semantic model to unrelated schema changes
Not recognizing that a view is still a live query, not a copy, so it adds no real performance overhead
Letting each report author re-derive the same business logic slightly differently instead of standardizing it in a view
Treating the view layer as purely cosmetic rather than a genuine stability and consistency boundary
keyPoints: A view provides a stable contract, decoupling Power BI from base table schema changes
Business logic defined once in a view avoids multiple slightly-different report-level definitions
A view is a live query, not a data copy, so there's no meaningful performance tradeoff
The real cost is an added layer to maintain and document

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recommends a view layer with clear reasoning
Correctly explains the schema-decoupling benefit
Correctly explains the consistent-business-logic benefit
Acknowledges the real tradeoff (maintenance overhead)

questions.title: Laying Out a Star Schema for a New Subject Area
questions.prompt: Your company wants a new Power BI report on customer support tickets: each ticket has an open date, a close date, an assigned agent, a customer, a priority level, and a resolution time. Sketch how you'd split this into fact and dimension tables, and explain your reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer: The core decision is separating what happened (the event) from what describes it (the entities). A fact table, something like FactTickets, should hold one row per ticket with foreign keys pointing to dimension tables — DateKey (or two: OpenDateKey and CloseDateKey, since both are meaningful separately), AgentKey, CustomerKey, PriorityKey — plus the numeric measure, ResolutionTimeMinutes, that reports will aggregate. Dimension tables then hold the descriptive, slowly-changing attributes: DimAgent (agent name, team, hire date), DimCustomer (name, segment, region), DimPriority (priority label, SLA target), and a shared DimDate used for both the open and close dates via two separate relationships. The reasoning follows the fact/dimension shortcut directly: anything answering "what happened, how much, how many" (a ticket occurring, its resolution time) belongs in the fact table, while anything answering "what is this thing called, what category is it" (an agent's name, a customer's region) belongs in a dimension, normalized rather than repeated on every ticket row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by asking, for every piece of information in the request, 'is this an event or a thing?' A ticket being opened is clearly an event — that's the fact table, FactTickets, one row per ticket. Resolution time is a number I'll want to aggregate across tickets, so that's a measure column sitting right on the fact table too. Everything else — the agent, the customer, the priority level — are things that describe the ticket, not events themselves, so each becomes its own dimension table: DimAgent, DimCustomer, DimPriority. The one wrinkle I'd flag explicitly is the two dates — open date and close date are both genuinely meaningful on their own, so I'd use a single shared DimDate table but relate it to the fact table twice, through two separate relationships (one of which would need to be set inactive, with USERELATIONSHIP used in DAX when a measure specifically needs to use the close-date relationship instead of the default active one). That's a real design decision worth calling out, not something to gloss over.
commonMistakes: Putting agent name or customer name directly on the fact table instead of normalizing into dimensions
Using only one DateKey when the ticket genuinely has two meaningful dates (open and close)
Forgetting that only one relationship to a shared DimDate can be active at a time, requiring USERELATIONSHIP for the inactive one
Mixing fact and dimension columns on the same table instead of keeping them cleanly separated
keyPoints: Fact table holds the event (ticket) plus its numeric measures and dimension keys
Dimensions hold descriptive attributes: agent, customer, priority
A shared DimDate can serve two date roles via two relationships, only one active at a time
The fact/dimension split follows 'what happened' vs. 'what is this thing called'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates fact (ticket event) from dimensions
Correctly identifies the dual-date relationship design decision
Proposes sensible, normalized dimension tables
Explains the fact/dimension reasoning clearly

questions.title: Static Roles or Dynamic RLS for a Growing Sales Org
questions.prompt: A sales organization currently has 5 regions and wants row-level security so each regional manager only sees their own region's data. The VP mentions the company plans to expand to 40 territories within two years. Would you design static RLS roles or dynamic RLS, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Dynamic RLS is the better design here, specifically because of the stated growth trajectory, even though static roles would technically work for 5 regions today. A static role defines one hardcoded filter per region (like [Region] = "West"), which means 5 regions require 5 separately created and separately maintained roles, each needing someone to manually assign the right people to it in the service. That approach doesn't scale cleanly to 40 territories — it means creating, testing, and maintaining 40 separate role definitions, and every org change (a new territory, a reassigned manager) becomes a manual update to a specific role rather than a data change. Dynamic RLS instead uses a single role whose filter expression, typically [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), adapts automatically based on who's signed in, paired with a user-mapping table that pairs each person's email with their assigned territory. Scaling from 5 regions to 40 territories becomes a matter of adding rows to the mapping table, not creating new roles — which is exactly the maintenance burden the company's stated growth plan makes worth avoiding from the start.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given that the VP specifically mentioned 40 territories are coming within two years, I'd build dynamic RLS now rather than static roles, even though static would technically get the job done for just 5 regions today. The real argument is maintenance cost as this scales: a static role is one hardcoded filter per region, which means 5 regions is 5 separate roles I have to build, test, and separately assign people to in the service — and that same approach at 40 territories is 40 of everything, with every reorg or new hire meaning someone has to remember which specific role to update. Dynamic RLS sidesteps all of that: one role, with a filter like UserEmail = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), checked against a small mapping table that just pairs each person's email to their territory. Going from 5 regions to 40 territories under that design is literally just adding rows to a table, not building new roles — which is exactly the kind of growth the VP described, so I'd rather build the dynamic version now than redo this work in a year under time pressure.
commonMistakes: Choosing static roles because they're simpler for the current 5 regions, without weighing the stated growth plan
Forgetting that the user-mapping table's identity format must match what USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns in the service specifically
Assuming Test as role can fully validate how a specific other person will see the report (it only tests using your own identity)
Not considering the ongoing maintenance cost difference between 5 static roles and 40 static roles
keyPoints: Static roles require one separately maintained role per region/territory
Dynamic RLS uses one role whose filter adapts via a user-mapping table
Scaling dynamic RLS is a data change (add a row); scaling static RLS is a design change (add a role)
The stated growth plan is the deciding factor, not the current count alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recommends dynamic RLS with correct reasoning tied to the growth plan
Correctly explains the static-role scaling problem
Correctly describes the dynamic RLS mechanism (mapping table + USERPRINCIPALNAME)
Frames the decision around future maintenance cost, not just current state

questions.title: Import or DirectQuery for a New Finance Semantic Model
questions.prompt: Finance wants a new Power BI semantic model against a 15 GB SQL Server finance database, and insists the numbers must be "accurate to the second" because of same-day reconciliation. Would you choose Import or DirectQuery, and what would you tell them about the tradeoff?
questions.modelAnswer: This genuinely leans toward DirectQuery, because the stated requirement — accuracy to the second for same-day reconciliation — is precisely the scenario DirectQuery exists for: it queries the source live on every visual interaction, so there's no refresh lag at all, unlike Import, which is only ever as current as its last scheduled refresh. The real tradeoff to communicate honestly is that DirectQuery's visual speed depends entirely on the source database's own query performance, not on Power BI, so a 15 GB finance database with well-tuned indexes might feel fine, while an unoptimized one could make every click noticeably slower than Finance is used to. DirectQuery also restricts some DAX and modeling features compared to Import. A fair way to frame the decision for Finance: if genuinely real-time accuracy is non-negotiable, DirectQuery is correct and any slowness is a database performance problem to solve separately (indexing, query tuning) — but if "accurate to the second" really means "accurate as of this morning's refresh is fine, we just don't want stale numbers from last week," Import with a more frequent scheduled refresh solves the actual underlying need with none of DirectQuery's performance dependency.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd actually push back gently on the requirement first, because 'accurate to the second' and 'accurate as of today' get used interchangeably by stakeholders more often than people realize, and the right architecture is genuinely different depending on which one Finance actually means. If they truly need live, second-by-second accuracy — someone's actively reconciling intraday and a stale number would cause a real problem — that's DirectQuery, full stop, because Import can only ever be as fresh as its last refresh. But I'd be upfront about the real cost of that choice: DirectQuery's speed is entirely at the mercy of the source database's own performance, so if that finance database isn't well-indexed for the kinds of questions this report will ask, every click in the report inherits that slowness, and that's a database tuning problem, not something Power BI itself can fix. If it turns out 'accurate to the second' really just means 'not stale from last week,' I'd recommend Import with a tighter refresh schedule instead, since it gets them effectively the same practical outcome with far better report performance and full DAX feature support.
commonMistakes: Choosing Import by default without clarifying what 'accurate to the second' actually requires
Choosing DirectQuery without warning Finance that its speed depends entirely on the source database's own performance
Assuming DirectQuery always performs worse than Import, rather than it depending on the source's tuning
Not considering that converting DirectQuery to Import later is possible, but never the reverse
keyPoints: DirectQuery queries the source live; Import is only as current as its last refresh
DirectQuery's visual performance depends entirely on the source database's own speed
Clarifying what the stakeholder actually means by 'real-time' changes the correct architecture
Import generally offers fuller DAX/feature support than DirectQuery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the Import vs. DirectQuery tradeoff
Makes a reasoned recommendation tied to the stated requirement
Flags the source-database-performance dependency honestly
Clarifies the ambiguity in 'accurate to the second' before committing

questions.title: Relationship, Join, or Data Blend for a New Returns Dataset
questions.prompt: You need to bring a new Returns dataset into an existing Tableau workbook that already has Orders connected. Each return references an Order ID. Would you connect Returns via a relationship, a join, or a data blend? Walk through your reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer: A relationship is the right default choice here. Orders and Returns both plausibly share the same underlying data source and relate cleanly on Order ID, and a relationship lets Tableau combine them only when a worksheet actually needs fields from both, aggregating each side to the level of detail that specific worksheet requires rather than immediately duplicating rows the way a row-level join would. A join should only be reached for if something a relationship genuinely can't express is needed — a non-equality join condition, or a case requiring the two tables to behave as one single flattened logical table for a specific performance reason — neither of which applies to a straightforward Order ID match. A data blend is the wrong tool entirely unless Returns actually lives in a separate, unrelated data source (a different database or file system) that can't be connected into the same data source as Orders at all; blending is reserved for genuinely separate sources, not for two tables that could just as easily be related or joined within one data source.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default here is a relationship, and I'd only move away from that if something specific ruled it out. Orders and Returns relate cleanly on Order ID, and that's exactly the case a relationship is built for — Tableau only combines the two tables when a worksheet actually asks for fields from both, and it aggregates each side appropriately for that worksheet instead of immediately multiplying rows together the way a join would. I'd only reach for an actual join if I needed something a relationship structurally can't do, like a non-equality condition, and that's not the situation described here. Data blending is the one I'd rule out fastest, because blending is specifically for combining two genuinely separate data sources — if Returns is sitting in the same database as Orders, or even just a different table I can connect to from the same data source dialog, there's no reason to blend instead of relating them properly within one data source. I'd only consider blending if Returns turned out to live somewhere Tableau literally couldn't connect to alongside Orders at all.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a join immediately, without checking whether a relationship already covers the need
Reaching for a data blend when both tables actually live in the same connectable data source
Assuming a relationship always behaves identically to a join, missing the aggregation-timing difference
Not checking for a genuine need (non-equality condition, forced single-table performance) before dismissing a join entirely
keyPoints: A relationship is the right default for two tables in the same data source matching cleanly on a key
A relationship avoids eager row duplication by aggregating per worksheet need
A join is reserved for cases a relationship genuinely can't express
Data blending is for genuinely separate, unconnectable data sources, not an alternative to relating within one source

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recommends a relationship as the default with correct reasoning
Correctly explains when a real join would be needed instead
Correctly explains why data blending doesn't apply here
Reasoning is grounded in Tableau's actual mechanics, not just preference

questions.title: Where Should a Margin Percentage Actually Live
questions.prompt: Three different reports all need a margin percentage (Profit/Revenue), and each one currently computes it slightly differently as a row-level column on the source data. Where should this calculation actually live, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The underlying problem is that a row-level calculated column for margin percentage is the wrong tool for what's actually a summary metric, and three slightly different implementations is the predictable symptom of that mismatch. A ratio like margin percentage should be computed as a ratio-of-sums at whatever level of aggregation a report is actually displaying it — Profit summed divided by Revenue summed for that grouping — which is exactly what a PivotTable calculated field does correctly, and exactly what a row-level column summed or averaged cannot do correctly at any subtotal level. The fix is to retire the three independent row-level columns and standardize on one shared definition: either a single PivotTable calculated field pattern documented and reused across all three reports, or, if a genuinely row-level per-transaction margin is separately needed for some other purpose, a well-documented calculated column kept distinct from any aggregate reporting use. The real architectural point is that a ratio metric needing to exist at multiple levels of aggregation belongs computed at each level it's needed, not baked into a row-level column that then gets summed or averaged incorrectly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out the real problem first, because it's not really 'these three reports disagree,' it's that row-level margin percentage was never the right shape for this calculation to begin with. Margin is fundamentally a ratio — Profit over Revenue — and the mathematically correct way to compute that ratio at any level of grouping is to sum the Profit, sum the Revenue, and divide those two sums, not to compute a percentage per row and then average or sum that percentage afterward, which is exactly the kind of thing that produces three subtly different numbers depending on how each report happened to implement it. My actual recommendation is to retire the row-level column in all three reports and replace it with one standard PivotTable calculated field, Profit/Revenue, used consistently everywhere this metric shows up — that guarantees every report is doing the identical ratio-of-sums calculation instead of three independent, slightly different approximations of the same idea.
commonMistakes: Treating margin percentage as a value that should live on the source data as a column, when it's fundamentally a summary ratio
Averaging or summing row-level percentages across reports instead of computing a true ratio-of-sums
Fixing the discrepancy by picking whichever of the three existing implementations seems closest to correct, instead of standardizing on the right approach
Not documenting the agreed definition somewhere all three report owners can reference going forward
keyPoints: Margin percentage is a ratio, correctly computed as sum(Profit)/sum(Revenue) at whatever grouping level is needed
A row-level column that's later summed or averaged cannot reproduce this correctly
A PivotTable calculated field computes the correct ratio-of-sums automatically
Standardizing on one shared definition prevents each report from quietly drifting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the row-level column as the architectural mismatch
Correctly explains ratio-of-sums as the right approach
Recommends standardizing via a shared calculated field pattern
Explains why the three reports drifted in the first place

questions.title: Designing an Incremental Nightly Load for a Growing Table List
questions.prompt: A data team currently has five Azure Data Factory pipelines, one hardcoded per source table, copying each table nightly. The table list changes every few months as new sources are added. Propose a better pipeline design, and explain the tradeoff it introduces.
questions.modelAnswer: Five hardcoded, nearly-identical pipelines is a maintenance burden that grows every time a table is added or removed, since each change means building and testing a whole new pipeline rather than updating a configuration value. The better design is a single parameterized pipeline driven by a Lookup activity that reads the current table list from a configuration source — a control table, or a config file — with firstRowOnly set to false so it returns every row as an array, feeding a ForEach activity whose Items reference that array. Inside the ForEach, a single Copy activity, parameterized by @item() for the table name, handles the actual copy for whatever table that iteration is on. Adding or removing a source table becomes a one-row change to the configuration table, with zero changes to the pipeline itself. The tradeoff is that debugging becomes slightly less direct: a failure now surfaces inside a generic loop iteration rather than a pipeline with that table's name baked into it, and sequential-vs-parallel execution has to be decided carefully across all five-plus tables at once rather than independently per pipeline, since they now share one loop's settings.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd consolidate all five into one pipeline, driven by configuration rather than hardcoding each table into its own copy of nearly identical pipeline logic. The pattern is a Lookup activity at the start, reading the current table list from a small control table with firstRowOnly set to false so I get the whole list back as an array, feeding directly into a ForEach activity. Inside that ForEach, one Copy activity does the actual work, parameterized by @item() for whichever table that iteration is currently on. The real win is that adding the team's sixth or seventh source table six months from now becomes a single new row in a configuration table, with nobody touching the pipeline itself at all. I'd be upfront about the tradeoff, though: when something breaks at 2 AM, the error now says 'the ForEach iteration for table X failed' instead of 'the CustomerTable pipeline failed,' which is a half-step less direct to triage, and I'd also have to make one deliberate sequential-vs-parallel decision that now applies to every table in the list together, rather than being able to tune each pipeline's concurrency independently like before.
commonMistakes: Keeping five separate pipelines and just accepting the growing maintenance burden
Forgetting to set firstRowOnly to false on the Lookup, which would return only one row instead of the full table list
Not acknowledging the debugging tradeoff this consolidation introduces
Defaulting to parallel execution for all tables without checking whether any share a destination or resource
keyPoints: A Lookup activity with firstRowOnly: false feeds a ForEach the full table list
A single parameterized Copy activity inside the loop replaces five hardcoded pipelines
Adding a new source becomes a configuration change, not a pipeline change
The tradeoff is less direct debugging and a shared concurrency decision across all tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes the Lookup + ForEach + parameterized Copy pattern
Correctly explains how this reduces future maintenance
Honestly identifies a real tradeoff this design introduces
Mentions firstRowOnly: false as a necessary Lookup setting

questions.title: Choosing a Branching and Review Strategy for a Small BI Team
questions.prompt: A three-person BI team currently all commits directly to main, and a bad DAX change recently broke a shared report with no warning. Propose a branching and review strategy for this size of team, and explain why you wouldn't recommend something heavier.
questions.modelAnswer: For a three-person team, the right fix is a feature-branch-plus-pull-request workflow, not a heavier process built for a much larger org. Each change — a new report, a DAX fix, a model update — gets its own short-lived branch instead of a direct commit to main; when the work is ready, a pull request opens against main, giving the other two team members a place to actually review the change (ideally with at least one required approval before merge is allowed) and a checkpoint where any automated checks can run before the change reaches the shared report at all. This directly addresses the actual incident described: a bad DAX change landing straight on main with no review step is exactly what a required PR review would have caught before it ever reached production. The reason not to recommend something heavier — multiple long-lived environment branches, a formal change-advisory board, mandatory multi-approver sign-off — is that process overhead scales with team size and risk, and for three people on one shared codebase, a single main branch protected by required PR review already closes the actual gap without adding ceremony nobody has the staffing to sustain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this simple and proportional to the team's actual size, which is three people, not thirty. The fix for what just happened is a straightforward feature-branch-and-pull-request workflow: nobody commits straight to main anymore, every change gets its own branch, and a pull request is what actually merges it into main — with at least one of the other two team members required to approve before that merge button unlocks. That alone would have caught the exact incident they just had, because a second set of eyes on a DAX change before it reaches the shared report is specifically the gap that let a bad change through unreviewed. I'd deliberately stop there, though, and not reach for something heavier like multiple persistent environment branches or a formal review board, because that's process built for a much bigger org with a much bigger risk surface — for three people, a single protected main branch with required PR review closes the real gap without adding a weight of ceremony nobody on a three-person team has the bandwidth to actually sustain.
commonMistakes: Recommending a heavy multi-branch or formal-board process disproportionate to a three-person team
Proposing feature branches without also requiring at least one reviewer's approval before merge
Not tying the recommendation directly back to the specific incident (an unreviewed bad DAX change)
Assuming any branching strategy alone (without a required review gate) would have prevented the incident
keyPoints: Feature branches plus required pull-request review directly addresses unreviewed changes reaching main
A required approval gate is what actually catches a bad change before it ships
Process weight should scale with team size and actual risk, not be maximized by default
The recommendation should connect explicitly back to the real incident described

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes feature-branch + required PR review workflow
Explains how this specifically would have caught the described incident
Justifies not recommending a heavier process for this team size
Recommendation is concrete and actionable, not vague

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: Explaining Why Two Reports Disagree
questions.prompt: A stakeholder emails you, confused: the regional sales dashboard and the finance team's monthly report show different total revenue for the same month, and they want to know which one is "wrong." Walk through how you'd investigate and then explain this to them.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as two separate problems: finding the actual technical cause, and then explaining it to a non-technical stakeholder without making them feel talked down to or stuck choosing a side. The investigation should check the concrete, common causes first — different date filters (calendar year vs. fiscal year, or a report still mid-refresh for today's data), different underlying definitions of "revenue" (gross vs. net of returns, or including vs. excluding tax), or one report using a measure with an unintended filter override via CALCULATE while the other uses a plain aggregation. Once the actual cause is identified, the explanation to the stakeholder should be concrete and specific rather than vague reassurance — not "they're both fine, just calculated differently," but naming the exact difference ("the finance report excludes returns processed after month-end close, the dashboard includes them as of today") and recommending which one is actually correct for their specific question, or whether both are legitimately answering slightly different questions.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't guess or reassure before I actually know what's different between them — I'd pull up both reports side by side and check the obvious things first: are they filtered to the exact same date range, are they both defined as gross revenue or is one net of returns, is one of them mid-refresh and showing a slightly earlier snapshot than the other. In my experience it's almost always one of those three, not some exotic bug. Once I actually know the answer, I'd go back to the stakeholder with something specific, not hand-wavy — something like 'the finance report is net of returns processed through month-end close, and the dashboard includes same-month returns that haven't been reconciled yet, so for anything involving final close numbers, finance's report is the one to trust.' I think the worst thing I could do here is say 'they're both correct, just different' without explaining why in concrete terms, because that leaves the stakeholder exactly as confused as they started, just with less confidence that I actually looked into it.
commonMistakes: Reassuring the stakeholder both reports are 'fine' without identifying the actual specific difference
Jumping to a technical explanation full of jargon before confirming what the stakeholder actually needs to know
Guessing at the cause instead of actually comparing the two reports' filters and definitions directly
Not following up with a recommendation on which number to actually use for their specific decision
keyPoints: Investigates concrete causes (date filters, revenue definition, refresh timing) before explaining anything
Names the specific, actual difference rather than giving vague reassurance
Translates the technical finding into plain language for a non-technical stakeholder
Recommends which number is correct for the stakeholder's actual question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a concrete, methodical investigation approach
Identifies realistic, specific causes of report discrepancies
Explains how the finding would be communicated in plain language
Closes with an actionable recommendation, not just an explanation

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time
